concept_tested: Membership of the prime element group of the cell
stem: The inorganic matter of a living cell is grouped into prime elements, secondary elements and trace elements. Which set of elements forms the prime elements?

distractor_rationale.A: Nitrogen belongs to the secondary elements; the student stretches the prime group to include it because these four are usually quoted together as the main elements of living matter.
distractor_rationale.C: These three are secondary elements, and the familiar fertiliser trio is mistaken for the group that builds the bulk of organic matter.
distractor_rationale.D: Iron, zinc and copper are trace elements needed in very small amounts, so they cannot form the prime group.

solution: Only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen are placed in the prime element group. They are the elements from which the bulk of the organic molecules of the cell is built.
formula_principle: Inorganic bioelements are grouped as prime elements (carbon, hydrogen, oxygen), secondary elements (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium, sulphur) and trace elements.
common_misconception: Students carry over the habit of listing carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen together and therefore treat nitrogen as a prime element.
difficulty_basis: One-step recognition or direct use of a single prescribed fact; low reasoning and distractor load

concept_tested: Discriminating a secondary element from a trace element
stem: Nitrogen and chlorine are both required by living cells, but they are placed in different groups of the inorganic matter of the cell. Which statement places both of them correctly?

options.A: Nitrogen is a secondary element and chlorine is a trace element
options.B: Nitrogen is a prime element and chlorine is a secondary element
options.C: Nitrogen is a prime element and chlorine is a trace element
options.D: Nitrogen is a trace element and chlorine is a secondary element

correct_answer_text: Nitrogen is a secondary element and chlorine is a trace element

distractor_rationale.B: The prime group is restricted to carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, and chlorine is required only in trace amounts, so both placements fail.
distractor_rationale.C: Chlorine is placed correctly, but nitrogen is promoted to the prime group, which contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
distractor_rationale.D: The two groups are interchanged: nitrogen is a secondary element while chlorine is one of the trace elements.

solution: Nitrogen is listed with the secondary elements and chlorine with the trace elements, so this is the only pairing that matches the grouping of inorganic matter in the cell.
formula_principle: Secondary elements are nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulphur; trace elements include boron, chlorine, zinc, copper, iron, sodium, molybdenum, nickel, silicon and cobalt.
common_misconception: Because nitrogen is a constituent of proteins and nucleic acids, students assume it must rank with carbon, hydrogen and oxygen as a prime element.

stem: Consider the following three placements in the scheme of biomolecules of a living system. I. Polynucleotides are macromolecules. II. Glycerol is a micromolecule. III. Alkaloids are macromolecules. Which of these placements are correct?

distractor_rationale.B: Polynucleotides are indeed macromolecules, so rejecting the first placement is wrong, and alkaloids are secondary metabolites.
distractor_rationale.C: The placement of alkaloids is the faulty one; they belong to the secondary metabolites, which form a group of their own.

common_misconception: Students treat every organic substance with an unfamiliar name as a large polymer and so file alkaloids with the macromolecules instead of with the secondary metabolites.

stem: The matter of a living cell is first divided into organic and inorganic. Where do essential oils and lectins belong in this scheme?

options.D: Inorganic matter, along with the trace elements

concept_tested: Defining features of secondary metabolites and the organisms producing them
stem: Consider the following statements about secondary metabolites. I. They are small organic molecules. II. They are essential for the growth, development and reproduction of the organism that produces them. III. They are produced by several bacteria, fungi and plants. Which statements are correct?

distractor_rationale.B: A secondary metabolite is by definition not essential for growth, development and reproduction, so the second statement contradicts the definition.
distractor_rationale.C: The claim of essentiality is the false one; describing these molecules as small and organic is part of their definition.
distractor_rationale.D: Accepting all three ignores that these molecules are singled out precisely because the organism can grow, develop and reproduce without them.

solution: Secondary metabolites are small organic molecules made by several bacteria, fungi and plants, and they are not required for the growth, development or reproduction of the producer, which is what makes them secondary.
formula_principle: Secondary metabolites are small organic molecules produced by organisms that are not essential for their growth, development and reproduction, and are produced by several bacteria, fungi and plants.
common_misconception: Students reason that anything an organism spends energy making must be essential to it, and therefore accept the statement that secondary metabolites are needed for growth and reproduction.

concept_tested: Hydrogen to oxygen ratio implied by the general formula of carbohydrates
stem: Carbohydrates have the general formula (CH2O)n. What is the ratio of hydrogen atoms to oxygen atoms in such a molecule, and which familiar substance shows the same ratio?

options.D: 2:1, the ratio found in carbon dioxide

distractor_rationale.A: The ratio has been inverted; each CH2O unit carries two hydrogen atoms for one oxygen atom.
distractor_rationale.C: Water is H2O and already has two hydrogen atoms per oxygen atom, so a 1:1 ratio matches neither water nor the general formula.
distractor_rationale.D: The ratio is right but carbon dioxide contains no hydrogen at all, so it cannot show any hydrogen to oxygen ratio.

solution: Every repeating CH2O unit contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, giving a 2:1 ratio throughout the molecule, which is exactly the ratio of hydrogen to oxygen in water.
formula_principle: In the general formula (CH2O)n the hydrogen and oxygen atoms are present in the ratio 2:1, the same ratio as in water.
common_misconception: Students recall that carbohydrates are linked with water in this ratio but reverse it to 1:2, or attach the ratio to carbon dioxide because both carbon and oxygen appear in the formula.
difficulty_basis: One-step recognition or direct use of a single prescribed fact; low reasoning and distractor load

concept_tested: Testing candidate molecular formulae against the general formula (CH2O)n
stem: Which of the following molecular formulae is consistent with the general formula (CH2O)n for a carbohydrate?

distractor_rationale.A: Twelve hydrogen atoms against five oxygen atoms is not a 2:1 ratio; twelve hydrogen atoms would need six oxygen atoms.
distractor_rationale.B: Here hydrogen is fewer than twice oxygen, so the repeating unit CH2O does not fit.
distractor_rationale.D: Carbon and oxygen must be equal in number for the unit CH2O to repeat a whole number of times, and here they are not.

solution: In C5H10O5 the carbon and oxygen atoms are equal at five each and the hydrogen atoms are exactly twice that number, so the formula can be written as (CH2O)5.
formula_principle: A formula fits (CH2O)n only when carbon, hydrogen and oxygen are in the ratio 1:2:1, that is when carbon equals oxygen and hydrogen is twice either of them.
common_misconception: Students check only the hydrogen to oxygen ratio and forget that the carbon count must equal the oxygen count for the unit CH2O to repeat.

concept_tested: Deducing the monosaccharide series and the oxygen count from the hydrogen count
stem: A monosaccharide obeys the general formula (CH2O)n and one of its molecules contains 10 hydrogen atoms. To which series does this sugar belong, and how many oxygen atoms does one molecule contain?

distractor_rationale.A: The series is worked out correctly but the oxygen count is taken equal to the hydrogen count instead of half of it.
distractor_rationale.B: Ten hydrogen atoms give n equal to 5, not 6; a hexose would carry twelve hydrogen atoms.
distractor_rationale.D: Halving the hydrogen count gives 5, so taking n as 4 understates the molecule, which would then have only eight hydrogen atoms.

solution: Ten hydrogen atoms means 2n = 10, so n = 5. A sugar with five carbon atoms is a pentose, and it contains five oxygen atoms, as in C5H10O5.
formula_principle: In (CH2O)n the number of hydrogen atoms is 2n while the number of carbon and of oxygen atoms is n each; the series is named from the carbon count.
common_misconception: Students set n equal to the hydrogen count instead of half of it, and so report both the series and the oxygen count too high.
difficulty_basis: One comparison, short interpretation or routine calculation linking up to two prescribed facts

concept_tested: Naming the seven carbon monosaccharide and computing its hydrogen count
stem: A monosaccharide named in the classification of carbohydrates contains 7 carbon atoms per molecule and obeys the general formula (CH2O)n. Which sugar is it, and how many hydrogen atoms does one of its molecules contain?

distractor_rationale.A: The sugar is named correctly, but the hydrogen count is taken equal to the carbon count, whereas each CH2O unit carries two hydrogen atoms.
distractor_rationale.B: Twelve hydrogen atoms belong to a six carbon sugar; the hexose value has been carried over to a seven carbon sugar.
distractor_rationale.C: Erythrose is the four carbon tetrose, so it cannot be the seven carbon member of the series even though the arithmetic is right.

solution: Seven carbon atoms place the sugar in the heptose group, whose named example is sedoheptulose. With n = 7 the molecule carries 2 x 7 = 14 hydrogen atoms, giving C7H14O7.
formula_principle: A seven carbon monosaccharide is a heptose, whose named example is sedoheptulose; in (CH2O)n with n = 7 the hydrogen atoms number 2n.
common_misconception: Students either fail to link the carbon number to the correct series name or assume that carbon and hydrogen occur in equal numbers in a sugar.
difficulty_basis: Multi-part interpretation, pathway reasoning or calculation linking several facts with plausible traps

stem: Glyceraldehyde is the named example of which group of monosaccharides?

concept_tested: Identifying a disaccharide from its atom counts and its hydrolysis products
stem: A carbohydrate Z contains 12 carbon atoms, 22 hydrogen atoms and 11 oxygen atoms per molecule. On hydrolysis Z yields two hexose units, one of which is fructose. Which statement about Z is correct?

options.A: Z is maltose, and its hydrogen to oxygen ratio is 2:1
options.B: Z is sucrose, and its hydrogen to oxygen ratio is greater than 2:1
options.C: Z is lactose, and its hydrogen to oxygen ratio is 1:1
options.D: Z is sucrose, and its hydrogen to oxygen ratio is 2:1

correct_answer_text: Z is sucrose, and its hydrogen to oxygen ratio is 2:1

distractor_rationale.A: The ratio is worked out correctly, but maltose yields two glucose units on hydrolysis and never yields fructose.
distractor_rationale.B: The sugar is identified correctly, but 22 hydrogen to 11 oxygen reduces exactly to 2:1; a ratio greater than 2:1 is a feature of lipids, not of carbohydrates.
distractor_rationale.C: Lactose yields glucose and galactose rather than fructose, and 22 hydrogen atoms to 11 oxygen atoms is 2:1 and not 1:1.

solution: Dividing 22 hydrogen atoms by 11 oxygen atoms gives the 2:1 ratio expected of a carbohydrate. A disaccharide that yields two hexoses, one of them fructose, must be sucrose, which is glucose plus fructose.
formula_principle: Carbohydrates carry hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 2:1; sucrose is the disaccharide made of glucose and fructose, maltose of two glucose units and lactose of glucose and galactose.
common_misconception: Students either treat any twelve carbon sugar as maltose or, having identified sucrose, assume that a large sugar departs from the 2:1 hydrogen to oxygen ratio.
difficulty_basis: Extended synthesis across several claims, stages or calculations with high working-memory and trap density

concept_tested: Assigning three disaccharides from hydrolysis products and transport role
stem: Three disaccharides are described. X yields two molecules of the same monosaccharide on hydrolysis. Y yields glucose and galactose. Z is the form in which carbohydrate is transported in plants. Identify X, Y and Z.

options.A: X maltose, Y lactose, Z sucrose
options.B: X sucrose, Y lactose, Z maltose
options.C: X maltose, Y sucrose, Z lactose
options.D: X lactose, Y maltose, Z sucrose

correct_answer_text: X maltose, Y lactose, Z sucrose

distractor_rationale.B: Sucrose yields two different monosaccharides, glucose and fructose, and maltose is not the transported form in plants.
distractor_rationale.C: Sucrose yields glucose and fructose rather than glucose and galactose, and lactose is not moved through the plant body.
distractor_rationale.D: The first two are interchanged: lactose gives two different sugars while maltose gives two glucose units.

concept_tested: The linkage common to disaccharides, polysaccharides and nucleosides
stem: Maltose, starch and a nucleoside all contain the same kind of linkage, formed by condensation, holding a sugar unit to the group next to it. Which linkage is this?

distractor_rationale.A: A peptide bond joins the carboxyl group of one amino acid residue to the amino group of another and belongs to polypeptides.
distractor_rationale.C: Ester linkages join fatty acids to alcohols in simple lipids and do not link sugar units to one another.
distractor_rationale.D: Hydrogen bonds act between whole molecules, as in cellulose, but they do not join the sugar units within a chain.

formula_principle: The glycosidic bond, formed on condensation, holds monosaccharide units together and occurs in disaccharides, polysaccharides and nucleosides.
common_misconception: Students associate the glycosidic bond only with sugar to sugar links in disaccharides and look for a different name when a nucleoside is mentioned.

concept_tested: Counting glycosidic bonds in an unbranched chain of monosaccharide units
stem: An unbranched polysaccharide chain is built from 250 monosaccharide units joined one after another, each glycosidic bond holding two neighbouring units together. How many glycosidic bonds does this chain contain?

distractor_rationale.A: One bond is counted for every unit, but a chain of n units joined end to end has one bond fewer than the number of units.
distractor_rationale.C: The number of units is halved, as though each bond used up two units and no unit were shared between successive bonds.
distractor_rationale.D: An extra bond is added beyond the end of the chain, although the two terminal units are bonded on one side only.

solution: Each new unit added to an unbranched chain brings one new glycosidic bond, and the first unit brings none, so 250 units are held together by 250 - 1 = 249 glycosidic bonds.
formula_principle: One glycosidic bond holds two monosaccharide units together, so an unbranched chain of n units contains n - 1 glycosidic bonds.
common_misconception: Students match one bond to each unit and answer 250, ignoring that the two units at the ends of the chain are bonded on one side only.
difficulty_basis: One comparison, short interpretation or routine calculation linking up to two prescribed facts

concept_tested: Change undergone by the copper of Benedict's reagent with a reducing sugar
stem: Monosaccharides act as reducing sugars in Benedict's test. What change does the copper of Benedict's reagent undergo?

options.B: Cu2+ is converted to metallic copper
options.C: Cu+ is converted to metallic copper

distractor_rationale.A: This is an oxidation of copper, whereas the sugar acts as the reducing agent and so the copper of the reagent must be reduced.

formula_principle: A reducing sugar carries a free aldehyde or ketone group and reduces Benedict's reagent, in which Cu2+ is converted to Cu+.

concept_tested: Total glucose in a stated blood volume at the normal concentration
stem: The normal level of glucose in human blood is about 90 mg per 100 ml of blood. Taking this level, what mass of glucose is present in a total blood volume of 5 litres?

distractor_rationale.A: This is the amount in one litre of blood; the total volume of 5 litres has not been used.
distractor_rationale.C: The answer is ten times too large, as though 5 litres contained five hundred portions of 100 ml instead of fifty.
distractor_rationale.D: This assumes 5 litres to be 10000 ml, doubling the number of 100 ml portions in the given volume.

solution: 5 litres is 5000 ml, which contains 5000 / 100 = 50 portions of 100 ml. Each portion holds about 90 mg of glucose, so the total is 50 x 90 = 4500 mg, that is 4.5 g.
formula_principle: Total quantity equals concentration multiplied by volume; a concentration of 90 mg per 100 ml means 90 mg in each 100 ml portion of the blood.

stem: In cellulose, the sugar units within a single molecule are joined by one kind of bond, while neighbouring cellulose molecules are held to one another by a different kind of bond. Which combination is correct?

options.A: Hydrogen bonds within a molecule and glycosidic bonds between molecules
options.B: Glycosidic bonds within a molecule and peptide bonds between molecules
options.C: Glycosidic bonds within a molecule and hydrogen bonds between molecules
options.D: Ester bonds within a molecule and hydrogen bonds between molecules

correct_answer_text: Glycosidic bonds within a molecule and hydrogen bonds between molecules

distractor_rationale.A: The two are interchanged; the sugar units of any polysaccharide chain are joined by glycosidic bonds.

correct_answer_text: A fat is an ester of fatty acids with glycerol, while a wax is an ester of a long-chain fatty acid with a long-chain alcohol

concept_tested: Calculating hydrogen atom numbers from the stated hydrogen to oxygen ratios
stem: In carbohydrates the hydrogen to oxygen ratio is exactly 2:1, while in lipids it is greater than 2:1. Two molecules each contain 18 oxygen atoms. Molecule X is a carbohydrate and molecule Y is a lipid. Which statement about their hydrogen atoms is correct?

options.A: X has 36 hydrogen atoms and Y has fewer than 36
options.B: X has 36 hydrogen atoms and Y has more than 36
options.C: X has 9 hydrogen atoms and Y has more than 9
options.D: X has 36 hydrogen atoms and Y has exactly 36

correct_answer_text: X has 36 hydrogen atoms and Y has more than 36

distractor_rationale.A: The hydrogen count of X is right, but a ratio greater than 2:1 in the lipid must raise the hydrogen number above 36, not lower it.
distractor_rationale.C: The ratio has been inverted; 2:1 means twice as many hydrogen atoms as oxygen atoms, giving 36 and not 9.
distractor_rationale.D: If Y also had exactly 36 hydrogen atoms its ratio would be 2:1, which is the carbohydrate value and not the lipid value.

solution: For the carbohydrate the ratio is fixed at 2:1, so 18 oxygen atoms are accompanied by 2 x 18 = 36 hydrogen atoms. For the lipid the ratio exceeds 2:1 with the same 18 oxygen atoms, so its hydrogen atoms must number more than 36.
formula_principle: For a carbohydrate, number of hydrogen atoms = 2 x number of oxygen atoms; for a lipid, number of hydrogen atoms > 2 x number of oxygen atoms.
common_misconception: Students invert the ratio and divide instead of multiplying, or forget that 'greater than 2:1' fixes the direction of the difference.
difficulty_basis: Multi-part interpretation, pathway reasoning or calculation linking several facts with plausible traps

concept_tested: Combining solubility, hydrogen to oxygen ratio and molecular size for lipids
stem: Which statement about lipids as a group is correct?

options.A: They are insoluble in water, their hydrogen to oxygen ratio is greater than 2:1, and their molecular weight is smaller than that of the macromolecules
options.B: They are insoluble in water, their hydrogen to oxygen ratio is exactly 2:1, and their molecular weight is smaller than that of the macromolecules

options.D: They are insoluble in water, their hydrogen to oxygen ratio is less than 2:1, and their molecular weight is larger than that of the macromolecules

correct_answer_text: They are insoluble in water, their hydrogen to oxygen ratio is greater than 2:1, and their molecular weight is smaller than that of the macromolecules

formula_principle: Lipids are characterised together by water insolubility, a hydrogen to oxygen ratio greater than 2:1, and a molecular weight smaller than that of the macromolecules.

concept_tested: Contrasting the bonds that maintain secondary and tertiary structure
stem: Which comparison between the secondary and the tertiary structure of a protein is correct?

options.A: The secondary structure is held by disulphide bonds, while the tertiary structure involves hydrogen bonds
options.B: The secondary structure is held by peptide bonds, while the tertiary structure involves hydrogen bonds
options.C: The secondary structure is held by hydrogen bonds, while the tertiary structure involves disulphide bonds
options.D: Both the secondary and the tertiary structure are held only by peptide bonds

correct_answer_text: The secondary structure is held by hydrogen bonds, while the tertiary structure involves disulphide bonds

distractor_rationale.A: The two bond types are interchanged; the helices and pleated sheets are held by hydrogen bonds, not by disulphide bonds.
distractor_rationale.B: Peptide bonds link the residues of the chain itself and are not what distinguishes the secondary level from the tertiary level.
distractor_rationale.D: If only peptide bonds were involved there would be no basis for distinguishing the two structural levels at all.

solution: Hydrogen bonds maintain the alpha helix, beta helix and pleated sheet of the secondary structure, whereas the looping, twisting and folding back of the chain in the tertiary structure is due to disulphide bonds.
formula_principle: Secondary structure, comprising the alpha helix, beta helix and pleated sheet, is held by hydrogen bonds; tertiary structure arises when the chain is looped, twisted and folded back due to disulphide bonds.
common_misconception: Students learn that hydrogen bonds stabilise protein shape in general and extend that to every structural level.
difficulty_basis: One comparison, short interpretation or routine calculation linking up to two prescribed facts

concept_tested: Counting peptide bonds in a chain of the maximum stated length
stem: A protein may contain up to 3000 amino acid units. If a single unbranched polypeptide chain contains exactly this maximum number of amino acid units, how many peptide bonds does it contain?

distractor_rationale.A: This assumes one peptide bond per amino acid unit; the chain has one bond fewer than the number of units because the two ends are free.
distractor_rationale.B: This adds a bond beyond the two ends of the chain, which have no further residue to bond to.
distractor_rationale.D: This halves the number of units, as though each peptide bond consumed two units without sharing them with neighbours.

stem: Four landmarks in the study of nucleic acids are listed. I: Chargaff's generalisation about the base ratio of DNA. II: Isolation of nucleic acids from pus cells by Friederich Miescher. stem: Which of the following correctly distinguishes purines from pyrimidines?

options.A: Purines are single-ring bases and include adenine and guanine, while pyrimidines are double-ring bases and include cytosine, thymine and uracil
options.B: Purines are double-ring bases and include adenine and guanine, while pyrimidines are single-ring bases and include cytosine, thymine and uracil
options.C: Purines are double-ring bases and include cytosine and thymine, while pyrimidines are single-ring bases and include adenine, guanine and uracil
options.D: Purines are double-ring bases and include adenine and cytosine, while pyrimidines are single-ring bases and include guanine, thymine and uracil

distractor_rationale.D: Cytosine is wrongly grouped with adenine and guanine is wrongly grouped with the pyrimidines; only adenine and guanine are purines.

concept_tested: Positions on the pentose sugar at which the base and the phosphate are attached and the carbon involved in chain formation
stem: The backbone of a polynucleotide chain is made of alternate sugar and phosphate groups. In each nucleotide the nitrogenous base is attached to one carbon of the pentose sugar, the phosphate group to another, and a third carbon of the sugar is involved in linking the nucleotide into the chain. Which set of positions is correct?

options.A: Base at C-5, phosphate at C-1, chain linkage involving C-3
options.B: Base at C-1, phosphate at C-3, chain linkage involving C-5
options.C: Base at C-3, phosphate at C-5, chain linkage involving C-1
options.D: Base at C-1, phosphate at C-5, chain linkage involving C-3

correct_answer_text: Base at C-1, phosphate at C-5, chain linkage involving C-3

distractor_rationale.C: The base is placed at C-3, whereas C-3 is the carbon involved in the chain and C-1 carries the base.

formula_principle: Nucleotide architecture: the nitrogenous base joins the sugar at C-1, the phosphate at C-5, and C-3 of the sugar takes part in linking successive nucleotides.

concept_tested: Structural features of the double helix: diameter, spacing of nucleotide pairs, antiparallel chains and grooves
stem: Consider the following statements about the DNA double helix. I: Its diameter is 20 angstrom. II: The distance between two neighbouring nucleotide pairs is 34 angstrom. III: The two chains are antiparallel, the 3' end of one chain lying beside the 5' end of the other. IV: The helix shows a major groove and a minor groove. Which of the statements are correct?

formula_principle: Dimensions and features of the double helix: one complete turn 34 angstrom, distance between neighbouring nucleotide pairs 3.4 angstrom, diameter 20 angstrom, antiparallel chains, major and minor grooves.

concept_tested: Constancy of the (A+T)/(G+C) ratio within a species and its variation between species
stem: Chargaff observed that the base ratio (A+T)/(G+C) varies from one species to another but is constant for a given species. DNA is extracted from the liver cells and from the muscle cells of one animal, and also from the liver cells of an animal of a different species. Which result is expected?

options.A: The ratio differs between the two tissues of the one animal and is the same in the animal of the other species
options.B: The ratio is the same in all three samples, because it has a single fixed value for all living organisms
options.C: The ratio is the same in the two tissues of the one animal and may differ in the animal of the other species
options.D: The ratio differs in all three samples, because every cell of an organism has its own base ratio

correct_answer_text: The ratio is the same in the two tissues of the one animal and may differ in the animal of the other species

distractor_rationale.A: This reverses the observation; the ratio is a property of the species and does not change from tissue to tissue.
distractor_rationale.B: The ratio is constant only within a species; Chargaff found that it varies between species.
distractor_rationale.D: This denies the constancy within a species, which is the central part of Chargaff's generalisation.

solution: All cells of one species carry DNA of the same base ratio, so the liver and muscle samples of one animal give the same value, while an animal of another species may give a different value.
formula_principle: Chargaff's generalisation: the base ratio (A+T)/(G+C) is characteristic and constant for a species but varies between species.
common_misconception: Students read the phrase varies between species as meaning the ratio is variable everywhere, and expect different tissues of one animal to differ.

concept_tested: Calculation of adenine percentage in double-stranded DNA from a given cytosine percentage
stem: A sample of double-stranded DNA contains 22 per cent cytosine. What is the percentage of adenine in this sample?

distractor_rationale.A: This equates adenine with cytosine; adenine equals thymine, and cytosine equals guanine, so the two values need not be the same.
distractor_rationale.B: This is obtained by subtracting only the cytosine from 100 and halving the remainder, forgetting that guanine is also present at 22 per cent.
distractor_rationale.D: This is the combined percentage of adenine and thymine; it has not been divided between the two equal bases.

solution: Cytosine 22 per cent means guanine is also 22 per cent, so guanine and cytosine together are 44 per cent. The remaining 56 per cent is shared equally by adenine and thymine, giving adenine 28 per cent.
formula_principle: In double-stranded DNA, A = T and G = C, and the four bases together account for 100 per cent.
common_misconception: Students subtract only the stated base from 100 and forget that its complementary partner is present in the same amount.

concept_tested: Calculation of cytosine percentage in double-stranded DNA from a given (A+T)/(G+C) ratio
stem: In a sample of double-stranded DNA the base ratio (A+T)/(G+C) is 1.5. What is the percentage of cytosine in this sample?

distractor_rationale.B: This is the combined percentage of guanine and cytosine; it has not been divided between the two equal bases.
distractor_rationale.C: This is half of the adenine and thymine share, which belongs to adenine and to thymine, not to cytosine.
distractor_rationale.D: This is obtained by dividing 100 by the ratio 1.5 and then halving twice, which does not follow from the relation between the two base sums.

solution: If (A+T) is 1.5 times (G+C), then the two sums together equal 2.5 times (G+C), which must be 100 per cent. Hence (G+C) is 40 per cent, and since guanine equals cytosine, cytosine is 20 per cent.
formula_principle: In double-stranded DNA, A = T, G = C, (A+T) + (G+C) = 100 per cent, and the given ratio fixes the two sums.
common_misconception: Students stop at the combined guanine and cytosine value and report it as the cytosine percentage.

concept_tested: Total number of hydrogen bonds in a DNA segment from the numbers of the two kinds of base pair
stem: A segment of double-stranded DNA contains 40 adenine-thymine pairs and 60 guanine-cytosine pairs. An adenine-thymine pair is held by two hydrogen bonds and a guanine-cytosine pair by three. How many hydrogen bonds hold the two chains of this segment together?

distractor_rationale.B: This is obtained by giving three hydrogen bonds to the adenine-thymine pairs and two to the guanine-cytosine pairs, that is by interchanging the two values.
distractor_rationale.C: This counts two hydrogen bonds for all 100 pairs and ignores the extra bond of every guanine-cytosine pair.
distractor_rationale.D: This counts three hydrogen bonds for all 100 pairs and ignores that an adenine-thymine pair has only two.

common_misconception: Students apply a single bond number to every base pair instead of treating the two kinds of pair separately.

concept_tested: Reason why the equality of purines and pyrimidines does not hold for the hereditary material of tobacco mosaic virus
stem: The rule that purines and pyrimidines occur in equal amounts applies to DNA. A student extracts the hereditary material of tobacco mosaic virus and predicts that its adenine content will equal its uracil content. The prediction fails. Which explanation is correct?

options.A: The hereditary material of this virus is DNA, in which adenine pairs with thymine and not with uracil
options.B: The hereditary material of this virus is double-stranded RNA, in which adenine pairs with guanine
options.C: The hereditary material of this virus is RNA in which uracil has been replaced by thymine throughout
options.D: The hereditary material of this virus is single-stranded RNA, whose bases are not paired with those of a second chain

correct_answer_text: The hereditary material of this virus is single-stranded RNA, whose bases are not paired with those of a second chain

distractor_rationale.A: Tobacco mosaic virus has RNA, not DNA, as its hereditary material, so the pairing of adenine with thymine does not arise.
distractor_rationale.B: The RNA of this virus is single stranded, and adenine is a purine that does not pair with the purine guanine.
distractor_rationale.C: It is thymine that is replaced by uracil in RNA, not the other way round, and this substitution is not the reason the amounts differ.

solution: Tobacco mosaic virus has RNA as its hereditary material, and because this RNA is single stranded its bases are not paired with those of a partner chain, so purine and pyrimidine amounts are not equal.
formula_principle: Equality of purines and pyrimidines depends on complementary pairing between two chains, so it is not found in single-stranded RNA.
common_misconception: Students carry the base equality rule over from DNA to RNA simply by replacing thymine with uracil, without asking whether a second chain is present.

options.C: It is a linear polynucleotide forming about 3 per cent of the cellular RNA and carrying initiation and termination codons

formula_principle: Transfer RNA has 70 to 80 nucleotides, a clover-leaf shape described by Holley in 1965, four parts (DHU arm, amino acid binding site, anticodon loop, ribosome recognition site) and an amino acid attached at the 3' acceptor stem.

options.B: A catabolic pathway builds complex molecules from simpler ones, whereas an anabolic pathway breaks complex molecules down into simpler ones
options.C: A catabolic pathway builds complex molecules from simpler ones, whereas an anabolic pathway converts one molecule into another of the same size

stem: Which of the following correctly pairs a cellular event with the type of metabolic pathway to which it belongs?

options.A: Formation of a glycosidic bond between two monosaccharides - catabolic
options.B: Joining of amino acid residues by peptide bonds - catabolic
options.C: Breakdown of a polysaccharide into simple sugars - anabolic
options.D: Hydrolysis of sucrose into glucose and fructose - catabolic

correct_answer_text: Hydrolysis of sucrose into glucose and fructose - catabolic

distractor_rationale.C: Splitting a polysaccharide into simple sugars is a breaking-down event and belongs to a catabolic pathway.

formula_principle: Events that split larger molecules into smaller ones belong to catabolic pathways; events that join smaller molecules into larger ones belong to anabolic pathways.

options.B: Small organic molecules produced by several bacteria, fungi and plants that are not essential for their growth, development and reproduction
options.C: Small inorganic molecules produced by several bacteria, fungi and plants that are not essential for their growth, development and reproduction
options.D: Large organic molecules produced only by green plants that are not essential for their growth, development and reproduction

correct_answer_text: Small organic molecules produced by several bacteria, fungi and plants that are not essential for their growth, development and reproduction

formula_principle: Secondary metabolites are small organic molecules produced by several bacteria, fungi and plants and are not essential for the growth, development and reproduction of the producer.

concept_tested: Integration of the chemical group and precursor of cannabinol with the role of glucosinolates in cabbage
stem: Which of the following statements about secondary metabolites is correct?

options.A: Cannabinol is a phenolic synthesised from simple sugars, and glucosinolates give wine and chocolate their astringency
options.B: Cannabinol is a terpene synthesised from simple sugars, and glucosinolates are used as food preservatives
options.C: Cannabinol is a nitrogen-containing metabolite synthesised from mevalonic acid, and glucosinolates give chocolate its astringency
options.D: Cannabinol is a terpene synthesised from mevalonic acid, and glucosinolates give cabbage its flavour and protect it from pests

correct_answer_text: Cannabinol is a terpene synthesised from mevalonic acid, and glucosinolates give cabbage its flavour and protect it from pests

distractor_rationale.A: Cannabinol is a terpene and not a phenolic, and astringency in wine and chocolate is due to tannins rather than to glucosinolates.
distractor_rationale.B: The group of cannabinol is right but its precursor is mevalonic acid, and it is the antibiotics that serve as food preservatives.
distractor_rationale.C: The precursor is right but cannabinol belongs to the terpenes, and astringency in chocolate is due to tannins.

solution: Cannabinol belongs to the terpenes, which are synthesised from mevalonic acid, while glucosinolates are the compounds that give cabbage its characteristic flavour and guard it against pests.
formula_principle: Cannabinol is a terpene formed from mevalonic acid; glucosinolates are the secondary metabolites responsible for the flavour of cabbage and for its protection from pests.
common_misconception: Students assign cannabinol to the nitrogen-containing group because of its use as a drug, and credit glucosinolates with the astringency that belongs to tannins.
difficulty_basis: Extended synthesis across several claims, stages or calculations with high working-memory and trap density

concept_tested: Origin of the term enzyme from Buchner's cell-free yeast extract work
stem: Edward Buchner showed that an extract of yeast containing no living cells could by itself bring about fermentation of sugar. The term enzyme, which came into use from this work, is built from two Greek words whose combined literal meaning is:

distractor_rationale.B: The Greek zyma means yeast, not sugar; the student names the term after the substance fermented rather than after the source of the extract Buchner worked with.
distractor_rationale.C: The Greek en does mean in, but the second word is zyma, yeast. Reading the term as within the cell contradicts the very result Buchner obtained, which was fermentation without living cells.
distractor_rationale.D: Living ferment describes the older view that fermentation required intact living cells; the word enzyme was introduced precisely because that view had been set aside.

solution: Buchner found that yeast extract free of living cells still fermented sugar. The word coined from this work is built on the Greek en, meaning in, and zyma, meaning yeast, so the literal sense is in yeast.
formula_principle: Etymology of enzyme: en means in and zyma means yeast, following Buchner's demonstration of fermentation by cell-free yeast extract.
common_misconception: Students often assume the word enzyme refers to the intracellular site of action or to the sugar substrate, rather than to yeast, the material from which the active extract was obtained.
difficulty_basis: One-step recognition or direct use of a single prescribed fact; low reasoning and distractor load

concept_tested: Quantitative expression of the catalytic property using the sucrase figure
stem: Sucrase can hydrolyse about 100000 times its own weight of sucrose. A purified preparation contains 1 mg of sucrase. The mass of sucrose that this preparation can hydrolyse is about:

distractor_rationale.A: Obtained by using a factor of 10000 instead of 100000, or by dropping one power of ten while converting milligram to gram.
distractor_rationale.C: Obtained by multiplying by 1000 rather than 100000, a common slip when the milligram to gram conversion factor is used as the catalytic factor.
distractor_rationale.D: Obtained by carrying one extra power of ten, treating the factor as one million times the enzyme weight.

solution: 1 mg multiplied by 100000 gives 100000 mg of sucrose. Since 1000 mg make 1 g, this is 100 g of sucrose, which shows how a very small quantity of enzyme acts on a very large quantity of substrate.
formula_principle: Catalytic property of enzymes expressed quantitatively: mass of substrate acted upon equals the catalytic factor multiplied by the mass of enzyme, with 1 g equal to 1000 mg.
common_misconception: Students confuse the catalytic factor with the milligram to gram conversion factor and so lose or gain powers of ten in the final answer.
difficulty_basis: One comparison, short interpretation or routine calculation linking up to two prescribed facts

concept_tested: Recognising reversibility of action and specificity of action from described enzyme behaviour
stem: An enzyme catalyses the conversion of compound X into compound Y and also catalyses the conversion of Y back into X, and it acts on no substrate other than X and Y. Which two properties of enzymes are illustrated together by this behaviour?

options.A: Catalytic property and sensitivity to pH
options.B: Reversibility of action and specificity of action
options.C: Specificity of action and sensitivity to temperature
options.D: Reversibility of action and proteinaceous nature

correct_answer_text: Reversibility of action and specificity of action

distractor_rationale.A: Nothing in the description varies the pH of the medium, and the catalytic property alone does not account for the enzyme refusing all other substrates.
distractor_rationale.C: Specificity is correctly picked up, but no temperature is altered in the description, so sensitivity to temperature is not demonstrated.
distractor_rationale.D: Reversibility is correctly picked up, but the proteinaceous nature of the enzyme is a fact of composition and is not shown by the reactions described.

solution: Catalysing both the forward and the backward conversion of the same pair of compounds is reversibility of action, and acting on that pair alone and on no other substrate is specificity of action.
formula_principle: Properties of enzymes listed in the chapter: proteinaceous nature, three-dimensional conformation with an active site, catalytic property, specificity of action, reversibility of action, and sensitivity to temperature and pH.
common_misconception: Students treat every property in the printed list as demonstrated by any enzyme example and do not check which properties the given observation actually tests.
difficulty_basis: One comparison, short interpretation or routine calculation linking up to two prescribed facts

concept_tested: Dependence of catalytic ability on the three-dimensional conformation bearing the active site
stem: Rule: the catalytic ability of an enzyme depends on its three-dimensional conformation, which carries the active site. A globular enzyme is treated so that its three-dimensional folding is completely lost, while every peptide bond in the chain remains intact. What is the expected consequence?

options.A: The enzyme loses its catalytic ability, because the active site no longer exists
options.B: The enzyme retains its catalytic ability, because no peptide bond in the chain has been broken
options.C: The enzyme retains its catalytic ability but loses its specificity of action
options.D: The enzyme is converted into a cofactor for another enzyme

correct_answer_text: The enzyme loses its catalytic ability, because the active site no longer exists

distractor_rationale.B: Treats catalytic ability as a property of the unbroken chain itself; the chapter ties activity to the three-dimensional conformation that carries the active site, not merely to intact peptide bonds.
distractor_rationale.C: Assumes catalysis and specificity reside in different parts of the molecule, whereas both depend on the same active site formed by the folded conformation.
distractor_rationale.D: Cofactors are inorganic ions loosely attached to the protein part of a conjugated enzyme, so an unfolded protein cannot become one.

solution: The active site is created by the specific three-dimensional folding of the enzyme. Once that folding is lost the active site no longer exists, so the enzyme cannot bind its substrate or catalyse the reaction, even though the chain of amino acid residues is unbroken.
formula_principle: Structure and function relationship in enzymes: the active site is a feature of the folded three-dimensional conformation, so loss of that conformation abolishes catalytic ability even with the chain intact.
common_misconception: Students equate an intact polypeptide chain with an intact enzyme and expect activity to survive as long as no bond in the chain is broken.
difficulty_basis: Multi-part interpretation, pathway reasoning or calculation linking several facts with plausible traps

concept_tested: Naming the class of non-protein component to which NAD and FMN belong
stem: NAD and FMN occur as non-protein components attached to the protein part of certain conjugated enzymes. Such components are termed:

distractor_rationale.B: A cofactor is an inorganic ion such as magnesium, copper, zinc, iron or manganese, whereas NAD and FMN are organic molecules.
distractor_rationale.C: A prosthetic group is the component firmly bound to the protein component by chemical bonds, and the chapter lists it separately from the coenzymes, of which NAD and FMN are the named examples.
distractor_rationale.D: An activator is an inorganic substance that increases enzyme activity; it is discussed among the substances affecting activity, not as a component of a conjugated enzyme.

solution: The chapter names NAD and FMN as the coenzymes, the organic non-protein components attached to the protein part of a conjugated enzyme, and reserves the term cofactor for inorganic ions.
formula_principle: Classification of enzymes by composition into purely proteinaceous and conjugated enzymes, the non-protein part of the latter being a coenzyme, a cofactor or a prosthetic group.
common_misconception: Students use coenzyme and cofactor interchangeably and do not attach the organic versus inorganic distinction to the correct term.

concept_tested: Assigning FMN and a zinc ion to coenzyme and cofactor using the organic versus inorganic and tight versus loose criteria
stem: A conjugated enzyme is found to carry two non-protein components: an FMN molecule tightly attached to the protein part, and a zinc ion loosely attached to the protein part. In the terminology used in the prescribed account, these two components are respectively:

distractor_rationale.A: Reverses both criteria, calling the organic tightly attached FMN a cofactor and the loosely attached inorganic zinc ion a coenzyme.
distractor_rationale.B: It calls the organic FMN a cofactor, a term this chapter reserves for inorganic ions, and it calls the bound zinc ion an activator, which is a substance affecting activity rather than a component carried on the protein part.
distractor_rationale.C: FMN is correctly named, but an activator is an inorganic substance added to increase activity rather than a component held on the protein part of the enzyme.

solution: FMN is an organic molecule tightly attached to the protein part, which makes it a coenzyme, and zinc is an inorganic ion loosely attached, which makes it a cofactor. NAD is the other coenzyme example given, and magnesium, copper, zinc and iron are given as cofactor ions.
formula_principle: In this chapter, coenzymes are organic and tightly attached to the protein part while cofactors are inorganic ions loosely attached to it.
common_misconception: Students remember only that both terms name non-protein helpers and pick whichever term they met first, without applying the organic versus inorganic and tight versus loose tests.

distractor_rationale.A: Zinc is listed among the cofactor ions, but the ion associated with catalase in the chapter is iron.

concept_tested: Distinguishing a prosthetic group from a coenzyme by the nature of its attachment
stem: Rule: a conjugated enzyme carries a non-protein component in addition to its protein part, and the different kinds of non-protein component are told apart by the manner of their attachment. In one such enzyme the non-protein component is joined to the protein component by chemical bonds and cannot be separated from it without breaking those bonds. This component is best described as:

distractor_rationale.B: Coenzymes are described as tightly attached, and the word tightly tempts the student here, but attachment by chemical bonds that must be broken to separate the component is the description reserved for the prosthetic group.
distractor_rationale.C: Cofactors are inorganic ions loosely attached to the protein part, which is the opposite of firm attachment through chemical bonds.
distractor_rationale.D: An activator is an inorganic substance that raises enzyme activity when supplied to the reaction, not a bound component of the enzyme molecule.

solution: Firm binding to the protein component through chemical bonds is the defining description of a prosthetic group. Tight attachment of an organic coenzyme is not described in terms of chemical bonds that must be broken, and a cofactor is only loosely attached.
formula_principle: The chapter separates the non-protein components of conjugated enzymes by the manner of their attachment: coenzymes tightly attached, cofactors loosely attached, prosthetic groups firmly bound by chemical bonds.
common_misconception: Students treat tightly attached and firmly bound by chemical bonds as the same statement and therefore label every strongly held non-protein component a coenzyme.
difficulty_basis: Multi-part interpretation, pathway reasoning or calculation linking several facts with plausible traps

concept_tested: Identifying the class defined by covalent bond formation driven by hydrolysis of a compound
stem: Which functional class of enzymes creates covalent bonds between molecules using the energy obtained from the hydrolysis of a compound?

distractor_rationale.A: The similar name misleads the student; the lyases are represented in the chapter by aldolases, decarboxylases, dehydratases and fumarase, and are not described as bond-creating enzymes driven by hydrolysis of a compound.
distractor_rationale.B: Transferases such as glucokinase and glutamate pyruvate transaminase are grouped by the transfer of a group, not by the creation of covalent bonds using energy from hydrolysis.
distractor_rationale.C: Hydrolases such as amylases, proteases and sucrase carry out hydrolysis itself; the class in question uses the energy released by hydrolysis of a compound to make a bond.

solution: The ligases, also called synthetases, are the class described as creating covalent bonds with energy obtained from the hydrolysis of a compound. The chapter gives no named example for this class.
formula_principle: Definition of the ligases, also called synthetases, as the enzymes that create covalent bonds using energy obtained from the hydrolysis of a compound.
common_misconception: Students confuse ligases with lyases because the names are close, and also confuse a class that uses the energy of hydrolysis with the class that performs hydrolysis.

concept_tested: Multi-stage elimination to find the pair of enzymes drawn from two different functional classes
stem: Each of the following pairs consists of two enzymes listed in the prescribed account. In exactly one pair the two enzymes belong to different functional classes. Which pair is it?

distractor_rationale.B: Both aldolases and fumarase are listed among the lyases, so this pair lies within a single class.
distractor_rationale.C: Both amylases and nuclease are listed among the hydrolases, so this pair lies within a single class.
distractor_rationale.D: Both are listed as transferases, so this pair lies within a single class.

formula_principle: Functional classification of enzymes with named examples, applied in reverse: two enzymes share a class only if both appear under the same heading.

concept_tested: Correspondence of lock and key in Fischer's model to enzyme and substrate
stem: In the lock and key model put forward by Emil Fischer in 1894, the lock and the key stand respectively for:

options.C: The active site and the product

distractor_rationale.B: Reverses the analogy; the model treats the enzyme as the fixed lock and the substrate as the key that enters it.
distractor_rationale.C: The key hole, not the whole lock, represents the active site, and the product plays no part in the analogy as the chapter states it.

concept_tested: The essential difference of the induced fit model from the lock and key model
stem: Which statement expresses the essential difference of the induced fit model of Koshland from the earlier lock and key model?

options.A: The substrate alters its own shape so as to fit an unchanging active site
options.B: The approach of the substrate brings about a change in the conformation of the enzyme
options.C: The active site is already exactly complementary to the substrate before the substrate arrives
options.D: The enzyme acts on the substrate without forming an enzyme-substrate complex

correct_answer_text: The approach of the substrate brings about a change in the conformation of the enzyme

distractor_rationale.A: Places the flexibility in the substrate; the flexible model of Koshland places the conformational change in the enzyme.
distractor_rationale.C: This is the position of the lock and key model, in which the key hole is of the correct size from the outset, so it cannot be the point of difference.
distractor_rationale.D: Both models are accounts of how the enzyme-substrate complex is formed, so neither dispenses with it.

solution: In the induced fit or flexible model the enzyme is not rigid; the approaching substrate induces a change in the conformation of the enzyme so that the active site comes to fit it. Both models still describe the formation of the enzyme-substrate complex.
formula_principle: Induced fit or flexible model of Koshland, 1959: the approach of the substrate induces a conformational change in the enzyme, in contrast with the rigid complementarity assumed by the lock and key model.
common_misconception: Students think the induced fit model means the substrate is moulded to the enzyme, reversing which partner changes shape.

concept_tested: Detecting the induced fit idea wrongly imported into the lock and key model
stem: Rule: in the lock and key model only a key of the correct size and shape fits into the key hole. A student states that this model explains enzyme action by the enzyme changing its shape to accommodate the substrate. The correct evaluation of that statement is that it is:

options.A: Correct, because the key hole of the lock must widen a little before the key can enter it
options.B: Incorrect, because the lock and key model denies that any enzyme-substrate complex is formed at all
options.C: Incorrect, because a change of shape in the enzyme on substrate approach belongs to Koshland's model
options.D: Correct, because the two models describe the same conformational change in different words

correct_answer_text: Incorrect, because a change of shape in the enzyme on substrate approach belongs to Koshland's model

distractor_rationale.A: Extends the analogy beyond what it states; in the lock and key model the key hole is already of the right size and does not widen.
distractor_rationale.B: Reaches the right verdict for a wrong reason; both models are accounts of how the enzyme-substrate complex is formed.
distractor_rationale.D: Collapses the two models into one; the conformational change induced by the substrate is what separates the flexible model from the lock and key model.

solution: The lock and key model holds the active site to be already of the correct size and shape, so no change in the enzyme is required or described. A change in the conformation of the enzyme brought about by the approaching substrate is the feature of the induced fit or flexible model, so the student's statement misplaces it.
formula_principle: Lock and key model of Fischer assumes a pre-existing complementary active site, while the induced fit or flexible model of Koshland attributes a conformational change in the enzyme to the approach of the substrate.
common_misconception: Students merge the two models into a single account and credit the lock and key model with the flexibility that belongs to the induced fit model.
difficulty_basis: Multi-part interpretation, pathway reasoning or calculation linking several facts with plausible traps

concept_tested: Definition of Km as the substrate concentration giving half maximal velocity
stem: The Michaelis-Menten constant, Km, of an enzyme is defined as:

options.A: The concentration of substrate, in moles per litre, at which the enzyme becomes completely saturated
options.B: The concentration of enzyme, in moles per litre, at which the reaction attains its maximum velocity
options.C: The substrate concentration, in moles per litre, that gives half of the maximum velocity
options.D: The maximum velocity attained by the reaction when substrate is present in large excess

correct_answer_text: The substrate concentration, in moles per litre, that gives half of the maximum velocity

distractor_rationale.A: Complete saturation corresponds to the maximum velocity; Km corresponds to 50 per cent saturation of the enzyme with substrate.
distractor_rationale.B: Km is a substrate concentration, not an enzyme concentration, and it is fixed at half maximal and not at maximal velocity.
distractor_rationale.D: Confuses the constant with the maximum velocity itself; Km is expressed as a concentration in moles per litre, not as a rate.

solution: Km is a substrate concentration expressed in moles per litre, and it is the particular concentration at which the reaction runs at half of its maximum velocity.
formula_principle: Km, the Michaelis-Menten constant, is the substrate concentration in moles per litre that produces half of the maximum velocity, corresponding to 50 per cent saturation of the enzyme with substrate.
common_misconception: Students remember Km as being about half maximal velocity and therefore state it as a velocity rather than as the substrate concentration that produces that velocity.
difficulty_basis: One-step recognition or direct use of a single prescribed fact; low reasoning and distractor load

concept_tested: Comparing the substrate affinity of two enzymes from their Km values
stem: Enzymes P and Q act on the same substrate. Under identical conditions the Km of P is 2 x 10^-5 moles per litre and the Km of Q is 4 x 10^-3 moles per litre. Which conclusion follows?

options.A: Q has the greater affinity, because its Km value is the numerically larger of the two
options.B: P and Q must have equal affinity, because Km is fixed by the substrate and both act on the same one
options.C: Q attains half of its maximum velocity at a lower substrate concentration than P does
options.D: P has the greater affinity, because a lower substrate concentration gives half maximal velocity

correct_answer_text: P has the greater affinity, because a lower substrate concentration gives half maximal velocity

distractor_rationale.A: Reads a high Km as high affinity; the chapter states that a low Km means high affinity and a high Km means low affinity.
distractor_rationale.B: Treats Km as a property of the substrate; two enzymes acting on the same substrate can and do have different Km values.
distractor_rationale.C: Misreads the powers of ten: 4 x 10^-3 is the higher concentration, so Q needs more substrate, not less, to reach half maximal velocity.

solution: The Km of P, 2 x 10^-5 moles per litre, is lower than the Km of Q, 4 x 10^-3 moles per litre. P therefore reaches half of its maximum velocity at a much smaller supply of substrate, which is what high affinity for the substrate means.
formula_principle: Low Km means high affinity of the enzyme for its substrate and high Km means low affinity, because Km is the substrate concentration needed for half of the maximum velocity.
common_misconception: Students associate a larger number with a stronger property and so read the larger Km as the greater affinity, and they also compare 2 and 4 without comparing the powers of ten.
difficulty_basis: Multi-part interpretation, pathway reasoning or calculation linking several facts with plausible traps

concept_tested: State of the enzyme when substrate concentration equals Km
stem: An enzyme has a Km of 5 x 10^-4 moles per litre for its substrate, a value lying within the range of 10^-5 to 10^-2 moles reported for most enzymes. In an assay the substrate concentration is held at exactly 5 x 10^-4 moles per litre. At this concentration the enzyme is:

options.A: 50 per cent saturated with substrate and working at its maximum velocity
options.B: 50 per cent saturated with substrate and working at half of its maximum velocity
options.C: Completely saturated with substrate and working at half of its maximum velocity
options.D: 25 per cent saturated with substrate and working at half of its maximum velocity

correct_answer_text: 50 per cent saturated with substrate and working at half of its maximum velocity

distractor_rationale.A: Maximum velocity is reached only when the enzyme is saturated; at half saturation the velocity is half of the maximum.
distractor_rationale.C: Complete saturation would require a substrate concentration well above Km, and it corresponds to the maximum velocity, not to half of it.
distractor_rationale.D: Halves the saturation a second time; the chapter links Km directly with 50 per cent saturation of the enzyme with substrate.

solution: Km is by definition the substrate concentration producing half of the maximum velocity, and it corresponds to 50 per cent saturation of the enzyme with substrate. Since the assay concentration equals Km, both conditions hold together.
formula_principle: At a substrate concentration equal to Km the enzyme is 50 per cent saturated with substrate and the reaction runs at half of its maximum velocity.
common_misconception: Students separate the velocity statement from the saturation statement and pair half maximal velocity with full saturation, or full velocity with half saturation.
difficulty_basis: One comparison, short interpretation or routine calculation linking up to two prescribed facts

concept_tested: Interpreting the plateau of the substrate concentration curve as enzyme saturation
stem: The figure shows initial enzyme velocity plotted against substrate concentration while enzyme quantity, temperature and pH are constant. What accounts for the final, almost horizontal part of the curve?

options.A: The enzyme has begun to lose its conformation because the substrate concentration is very high
options.B: The substrate has been completely used up, so no further product can be formed in the assay
options.C: The reverse reaction has begun to run at a rate equal to that of the forward reaction
options.D: All the active sites of the fixed quantity of enzyme present are occupied by substrate

correct_answer_text: All the active sites of the fixed quantity of enzyme present are occupied by substrate

distractor_rationale.A: Loss of conformation follows unsuitable temperature or pH, both of which are held constant here; an excess of substrate does not unfold the enzyme.
distractor_rationale.B: The initial velocity is measured in each case, and the flat part of the curve lies at the highest substrate concentrations, where substrate is most plentiful.
distractor_rationale.C: A reverse reaction would show as a loss of product rather than as a ceiling on the initial velocity; the flat part reflects saturation of the enzyme.

solution: As substrate concentration rises, more and more active sites are occupied, so velocity climbs steeply at first. Once the fixed quantity of enzyme is saturated, no free active site is left, and further substrate leaves the velocity unchanged, which is why the curve becomes almost parallel to the x axis.
formula_principle: Effect of substrate concentration on enzyme activity: with the enzyme quantity fixed, velocity against substrate concentration is a rectangular hyperbola whose final phase is a plateau set by saturation of the enzyme.
common_misconception: Students read the plateau as exhaustion of the substrate or as damage to the enzyme, rather than as saturation of a limited number of active sites.
difficulty_basis: Multi-part interpretation, pathway reasoning or calculation linking several facts with plausible traps

concept_tested: Interpreting the rise and the sharp fall of the temperature curve of enzyme activity
stem: The figure shows the activity of a mammalian enzyme plotted against temperature while pH and substrate concentration are controlled. Which explanation of the curve is correct?

options.A: The optimum is 37 degree C, and above 40 degree C the enzyme denatures rapidly, most enzymes being destroyed at 60 to 70 degree C
options.B: The optimum is 65 degree C, and the fall in activity before it is caused by exhaustion of the substrate in the assay mixture
options.C: The rise reflects an increasing Km, and the fall begins once the Km of the enzyme has been exceeded by the temperature
options.D: The steep fall above 37 degree C occurs because heating shifts the pH of the medium away from the optimum for the enzyme

correct_answer_text: The optimum is 37 degree C, and above 40 degree C the enzyme denatures rapidly, most enzymes being destroyed at 60 to 70 degree C

distractor_rationale.B: Substrate is in large excess, and 65 degree C lies within the 60 to 70 degree C band in which most enzymes are destroyed, so it cannot be an optimum.
distractor_rationale.C: Km is a substrate concentration characteristic of the enzyme, not a temperature threshold, so it cannot mark the point at which activity falls.
distractor_rationale.D: The pH is held at the optimum throughout the experiment, so the loss of activity must be traced to the enzyme protein itself.

solution: Activity rises with temperature up to the optimum, which for reactions at normal mammalian body temperature is 37 degree C, the optimum range for most enzymes being 20 to 35 degree C. Beyond about 40 degree C the enzyme denatures rapidly, and by 60 to 70 degree C most enzymes are destroyed, which is why activity is negligible at 65 degree C.
formula_principle: Effect of temperature on enzyme activity: 37 degree C is the optimum for enzymatic reactions at normal mammalian body temperature, enzymes denature rapidly above 40 degree C, and most enzymes are destroyed at 60 to 70 degree C.
common_misconception: Students take the highest temperature at which any activity is seen, or the last point on the curve, as the optimum, and they look for causes outside the enzyme for the fall in activity.
difficulty_basis: Multi-part interpretation, pathway reasoning or calculation linking several facts with plausible traps

concept_tested: Identifying enzymes from their optimum pH values
stem: Two enzymes listed in the prescribed account are assayed over a range of pH values, with the temperature, the enzyme concentration and the substrate concentration identical in the two sets. One enzyme shows its maximum activity at pH 2 and the other at pH 9.5. The two enzymes are respectively:

distractor_rationale.B: Interchanges the two optima; the chapter gives pH 2 for pepsin and pH 9.5 for trypsin.
distractor_rationale.C: The first assignment is right, but the optimum of pH 9.5 is given for trypsin, and no pH optimum is given for amylase.
distractor_rationale.D: Both assignments fail: trypsin has its optimum at pH 9.5, not at pH 2, and no pH optimum is given for sucrase.

solution: Pepsin has its optimum at pH 2 and trypsin at pH 9.5, so the enzyme peaking in strongly acidic conditions is pepsin and the one peaking in alkaline conditions is trypsin.
formula_principle: Effect of pH on enzyme activity: each enzyme works best at a particular pH, pepsin having an optimum at pH 2 and trypsin at pH 9.5.
common_misconception: Students remember that the two enzymes have very different pH optima but cannot recall which enzyme takes the acidic value, and so reverse the pair.
difficulty_basis: One comparison, short interpretation or routine calculation linking up to two prescribed facts

concept_tested: Predicting which alterations of the reaction conditions lower enzyme activity
stem: An enzyme-catalysed reaction runs steadily at 37 degree C at the optimum pH, with substrate present in large excess. Four further assays are set up, each differing from this control in one respect only. In I a further quantity of the same enzyme is added. In II an inorganic activator is added. In III the temperature is raised to 65 degree C. In IV an inhibitor is added. In how many of the four assays is the activity expected to be LOWER than in the control?

distractor_rationale.A: Counts the inhibitor alone and overlooks that 65 degree C lies within the 60 to 70 degree C band in which most enzymes are destroyed.
distractor_rationale.C: Counts the addition of extra enzyme or of an activator as depressing activity, whereas an activator is an inorganic substance that increases enzyme activity.
distractor_rationale.D: Assumes that every departure from the control conditions must lower activity, ignoring that an activator raises it.

solution: Raising the temperature to 65 degree C places the enzyme in the 60 to 70 degree C band in which most enzymes are destroyed, so activity falls, and an inhibitor by definition reduces enzyme activity, so activity falls there too. Adding more of the same enzyme does not depress activity, and an inorganic activator increases it. Hence two assays show lower activity than the control.
formula_principle: Factors affecting enzyme activity: enzyme concentration, temperature with destruction of most enzymes at 60 to 70 degree C, and other substances, namely activators which increase activity and inhibitors which reduce it.
common_misconception: Students treat any change made to a working assay as harmful, and in particular do not distinguish an activator, which raises activity, from an inhibitor, which lowers it.
difficulty_basis: Extended synthesis across several claims, stages or calculations with high working-memory and trap density

concept_tested: Interpreting the plateau of an enzyme saturation curve
stem: In the enzyme-velocity graph shown, the curve becomes nearly horizontal at high substrate concentration. What does this plateau indicate?

options.A: Nearly all active sites of the available enzyme molecules are occupied
options.B: The substrate has converted the enzyme into a lipid
options.C: The reaction has become independent of enzyme concentration at every substrate level
options.D: The enzyme has necessarily been denatured by high temperature

correct_answer_text: Nearly all active sites of the available enzyme molecules are occupied

distractor_rationale.B: The substrate has converted the enzyme into a lipid is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required interpreting the plateau of an enzyme saturation curve and therefore cannot be the single correct response.
distractor_rationale.C: The reaction has become independent of enzyme concentration at every substrate level is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required interpreting the plateau of an enzyme saturation curve and therefore cannot be the single correct response.
distractor_rationale.D: The enzyme has necessarily been denatured by high temperature is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required interpreting the plateau of an enzyme saturation curve and therefore cannot be the single correct response.

solution: At high substrate concentration the fixed amount of enzyme becomes saturated, so nearly all active sites are occupied and adding more substrate produces little further rise in velocity.
formula_principle: A fixed enzyme concentration approaches a maximum velocity when its active sites are saturated.
common_misconception: A plateau from substrate saturation is confused with temperature denaturation.
difficulty_basis: One-step recognition or direct use of a single prescribed fact; low reasoning and distractor load

concept_tested: Inferring persistent activity loss after heating above the optimum
stem: An enzyme follows the temperature-activity curve shown. A sample is heated to 65 degree C and then cooled back to 37 degree C. Why may its original activity fail to return?

options.A: Cooling removes every substrate molecule from the solution
options.B: High temperature may irreversibly alter the enzyme's three-dimensional active site
options.C: The enzyme changes permanently into a carbohydrate at 65 degree C
options.D: Cooling forces all enzyme molecules to bind inhibitors

correct_answer_text: High temperature may irreversibly alter the enzyme's three-dimensional active site

distractor_rationale.A: Cooling removes every substrate molecule from the solution is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required inferring persistent activity loss after heating above the optimum and therefore cannot be the single correct response.
distractor_rationale.C: The enzyme changes permanently into a carbohydrate at 65 degree C is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required inferring persistent activity loss after heating above the optimum and therefore cannot be the single correct response.
distractor_rationale.D: Cooling forces all enzyme molecules to bind inhibitors is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required inferring persistent activity loss after heating above the optimum and therefore cannot be the single correct response.

solution: Heating well above the optimum can denature the protein and alter its active site. Cooling does not necessarily restore that three-dimensional structure.
formula_principle: High temperature can denature an enzyme, whereas ordinary cooling mainly slows molecular movement.
common_misconception: Students assume every temperature effect is fully reversible.
difficulty_basis: One comparison, short interpretation or routine calculation linking up to two prescribed facts

concept_tested: Combining GC percentage with hydrogen-bond counting
stem: A double-stranded DNA segment has 100 base pairs, of which 40 per cent are G-C pairs. How many hydrogen bonds hold the two strands together?

distractor_rationale.A: 180 is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required combining gc percentage with hydrogen-bond counting and therefore cannot be the single correct response.
distractor_rationale.B: 200 is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required combining gc percentage with hydrogen-bond counting and therefore cannot be the single correct response.
distractor_rationale.D: 300 is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required combining gc percentage with hydrogen-bond counting and therefore cannot be the single correct response.

solution: There are 40 G-C pairs and 60 A-T pairs. The total is 40 x 3 + 60 x 2 = 120 + 120 = 240 hydrogen bonds.
formula_principle: Each G-C pair has three hydrogen bonds and each A-T pair has two.
common_misconception: The percentage is applied to individual bases instead of base pairs, or one bond value is used for every pair.

concept_tested: Separating effects of concentration, inhibitor and denaturation
stem: Four assays begin with the same enzyme activity. I receives more enzyme while substrate remains abundant. II receives a specific inhibitor. III is heated to 65 degree C. IV receives more substrate when its enzyme is already saturated. In which assays is activity expected to decrease?

distractor_rationale.A: I and IV only is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required separating effects of concentration, inhibitor and denaturation and therefore cannot be the single correct response.
distractor_rationale.B: I, II and III only is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required separating effects of concentration, inhibitor and denaturation and therefore cannot be the single correct response.
distractor_rationale.C: II and IV only is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required separating effects of concentration, inhibitor and denaturation and therefore cannot be the single correct response.

solution: A specific inhibitor lowers activity and heating to 65 degree C can denature the enzyme. More enzyme with abundant substrate increases capacity, while more substrate at saturation causes little change rather than a decrease.
formula_principle: Enzyme activity is reduced by inhibitors and denaturing temperatures; saturation limits the effect of additional substrate.
common_misconception: A plateau is treated as a fall in activity, or adding enzyme is assumed to dilute the reaction.

concept_tested: Recall of the three ways in which ATP is formed by phosphorylation
stem: ATP is formed by phosphorylation, which is stated to occur in three ways. Which set names all three?

options.A: Photophosphorylation, substrate-level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
options.C: Substrate-level phosphorylation, oxidative phosphorylation and terminal oxidation

correct_answer_text: Photophosphorylation, substrate-level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation

distractor_rationale.B: Chemiosmosis is the name given to proton transfer across the inner mitochondrial membrane accompanied by ATP synthesis; it is not listed as a separate mode of phosphorylation.
distractor_rationale.C: Terminal oxidation is the step in which reduced oxygen combines with protons to give metabolic water; it is a step of aerobic respiration, not a mode of ATP formation.
distractor_rationale.D: Dehydrogenation is the removal of hydrogen from a respiratory material by dehydrogenases; no phosphate group is transferred to ADP in it.

solution: The three ways of forming ATP by phosphorylation are photophosphorylation, which occurs during photosynthesis, substrate-level phosphorylation, and oxidative phosphorylation.
formula_principle: ATP formation occurs by phosphorylation of ADP, and phosphorylation is of three kinds: photophosphorylation, substrate-level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation.
common_misconception: Students treat chemiosmosis or terminal oxidation as a fourth or a substitute mode of phosphorylation instead of as parts of the electron transport process.
difficulty_basis: One-step recognition or direct use of a single prescribed fact; low reasoning and distractor load
