concept_tested: Definition of substrate-level phosphorylation as distinct from the other modes
stem: Which statement correctly defines substrate-level phosphorylation?

options.A: Direct phosphorylation of ADP by transfer of a phosphate group from a suitable substrate
options.B: Phosphorylation of ADP at the cost of energy released during oxidation of NADH+H+ and FADH2
options.C: Phosphorylation of ADP using energy trapped during photosynthesis
options.D: Phosphorylation of glucose by transfer of a phosphate group from ATP

correct_answer_text: Direct phosphorylation of ADP by transfer of a phosphate group from a suitable substrate

distractor_rationale.B: This is the definition of oxidative phosphorylation, in which the phosphate is not handed over by the substrate itself but is added using energy from coenzyme oxidation.
distractor_rationale.C: This describes photophosphorylation, the mode that operates in photosynthesis and not in respiration.
distractor_rationale.D: This is the hexokinase reaction of glycolysis; here the substrate is phosphorylated and ATP is consumed, which is the reverse of ATP formation.

solution: In substrate-level phosphorylation the phosphate group comes straight from a phosphorylated substrate and is handed to ADP, so ATP is formed without any coenzyme oxidation.
formula_principle: Substrate-level phosphorylation is defined as the direct phosphorylation of ADP by transfer of a phosphate group from any suitable substrate.
common_misconception: Students confuse the molecule being phosphorylated, thinking that any transfer of a phosphate group in the pathway counts as substrate-level phosphorylation even when it is glucose and not ADP that receives the phosphate.
difficulty_basis: One-step recognition or direct use of a single prescribed fact; low reasoning and distractor load

concept_tested: Distinguishing the energy source and the site of oxidative phosphorylation from those of substrate-level phosphorylation
stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes oxidative phosphorylation from substrate-level phosphorylation?

options.A: Oxidative phosphorylation uses energy released when NADH+H+ and FADH2 are oxidised, and occurs on the inner mitochondrial membrane
options.B: Oxidative phosphorylation transfers a phosphate group straight from a substrate to ADP, and occurs in the cytoplasm
options.C: Oxidative phosphorylation occurs in the mitochondrial matrix, while substrate-level phosphorylation occurs on the inner mitochondrial membrane
options.D: Oxidative phosphorylation adds a phosphate group to the respiratory substrate rather than to ADP

correct_answer_text: Oxidative phosphorylation uses energy released when NADH+H+ and FADH2 are oxidised, and occurs on the inner mitochondrial membrane

distractor_rationale.B: The direct transfer of a phosphate group from a substrate is substrate-level phosphorylation; this option attaches that mechanism to the wrong mode.
distractor_rationale.C: The sites are interchanged; the matrix is the site of the Krebs cycle and the inner mitochondrial membrane carries oxidative phosphorylation.
distractor_rationale.D: In both modes it is ADP that receives the phosphate group; molecular oxygen serves as the final electron acceptor and does not phosphorylate the substrate.

solution: The defining features of oxidative phosphorylation are its energy source, the oxidation of the reduced coenzymes NADH+H+ and FADH2, and its location on the inner mitochondrial membrane.
formula_principle: Oxidative phosphorylation is phosphorylation of ADP at the cost of energy released during oxidation of substrates like NADH+H+ and FADH2, and is located on the inner mitochondrial membrane; substrate-level phosphorylation is direct transfer of a phosphate group from a substrate to ADP.
common_misconception: Students remember that both modes make ATP but interchange the site, placing oxidative phosphorylation in the matrix alongside the Krebs cycle.
difficulty_basis: One comparison, short interpretation or routine calculation linking up to two prescribed facts

subtopic: Substrate-level phosphorylation in the balance sheet
concept_tested: Adding the substrate-level contributions of glycolysis and of two turns of the Krebs cycle
stem: In the aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule, glycolysis yields 4 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, and one GTP (ATP) is formed by substrate-level phosphorylation for every molecule of citric acid oxidised. One glucose gives two turns of the Krebs cycle. How many ATP molecules arise by substrate-level phosphorylation per glucose?

distractor_rationale.A: This counts only the glycolytic contribution and omits the one GTP (ATP) formed in each of the two turns of the Krebs cycle.
distractor_rationale.B: This counts only the two turns of the Krebs cycle and omits the four ATP formed at the two ATP-yielding conversions of glycolysis.
distractor_rationale.D: 8 is the net benefit entered for glycolysis alone, which already includes the ATP credited to oxidative phosphorylation of the two NADH+H+.

solution: Glycolysis contributes 4 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and each of the two turns of the Krebs cycle contributes 1, so 4 + 2 = 6 ATP arise by substrate-level phosphorylation per glucose.
formula_principle: Total ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation per glucose = ATP from glycolysis (4) + one GTP (ATP) per turn of the Krebs cycle x 2 turns (2).
common_misconception: Students forget that one glucose drives two turns of the Krebs cycle and so credit only a single GTP (ATP) to the cycle, or ignore the cycle contribution altogether.
difficulty_basis: One comparison, short interpretation or routine calculation linking up to two prescribed facts

subtopic: Oxidative phosphorylation in the balance sheet
concept_tested: Converting the reduced coenzymes of one glucose into ATP using the accounting of the balance sheet and finding the gross total
stem: The balance sheet for ATP by aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule accounts each NADH+H+ as 3 ATP and each FADH2 as 2 ATP. Complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose delivers 10 NADH+H+ and 2 FADH2 to the electron transport system, and substrate-level phosphorylation contributes 6 ATP. How many ATP come from oxidative phosphorylation, and what is the gross total?

distractor_rationale.A: This values only the NADH+H+ and leaves out the 2 FADH2, and it also mistakes the net figure for the gross total.
distractor_rationale.C: The oxidative contribution is right but 38 is the net figure obtained after subtracting the 2 ATP consumed in glycolysis, not the gross total.
distractor_rationale.D: This values every reduced coenzyme at 2 ATP, applying the FADH2 factor to NADH+H+ as well.

solution: The 10 NADH+H+ account for 10 x 3 = 30 ATP and the 2 FADH2 for 2 x 2 = 4 ATP, giving 34 by oxidative phosphorylation; adding the 6 ATP from substrate-level phosphorylation gives a gross total of 40 ATP.
formula_principle: Oxidative phosphorylation ATP = (number of NADH+H+ x 3) + (number of FADH2 x 2); gross total = oxidative phosphorylation ATP + substrate-level phosphorylation ATP.
common_misconception: Students apply one conversion factor to both reduced coenzymes, or quote the net figure of the balance sheet when the gross total is asked for.
difficulty_basis: Extended synthesis across several claims, stages or calculations with high working-memory and trap density

subtopic: Identifying the mode of phosphorylation from the reaction
concept_tested: Recognising that an ATP-forming step inside the mitochondrion need not be oxidative phosphorylation
stem: Oxidative phosphorylation is defined as phosphorylation of ADP at the cost of energy released during oxidation of substrates like NADH+H+ and FADH2, and it is located on the inner mitochondrial membrane. In the Krebs cycle, which runs in the mitochondrial matrix, the conversion of succinyl-CoA to succinate yields one GTP (ATP). By which mode is that ATP formed?

distractor_rationale.A: The reaction is placed inside the mitochondrion, but no reduced coenzyme is oxidised on the inner membrane to drive it, so it does not meet the stated definition.
distractor_rationale.B: Photophosphorylation occurs during photosynthesis and has no role in any step of the Krebs cycle.
distractor_rationale.C: Chemiosmosis is the synthesis of ATP that accompanies the channelling of protons through the F0 part of the oxysome, which is not involved in this cycle step.

solution: In the succinyl-CoA to succinate conversion the phosphate group reaches the nucleotide directly from the substrate, so the ATP is formed by substrate-level phosphorylation even though the reaction takes place inside the mitochondrion.
formula_principle: The mode of ATP formation is decided by the mechanism of phosphate transfer, not by the compartment in which the reaction happens.
common_misconception: Students assume that every ATP made inside the mitochondrion must come from oxidative phosphorylation and that substrate-level phosphorylation is confined to the cytoplasm.
difficulty_basis: Multi-part interpretation, pathway reasoning or calculation linking several facts with plausible traps

concept_tested: Recall of the cellular compartment in which glycolysis occurs
stem: In which part of the cell does glycolysis take place?

distractor_rationale.A: The mitochondrial matrix is the site of the Krebs cycle, which follows glycolysis and the connecting link reaction.
distractor_rationale.C: The inner mitochondrial membrane carries the electron transport complexes and oxidative phosphorylation, not the glycolytic enzymes.
distractor_rationale.D: The outer chamber is where protons are released during oxidation of NADH+H+ and FADH2; no reaction of glycolysis occurs there.

solution: All ten steps of glycolysis, from glucose to pyruvic acid, take place in the cytoplasm of the cell.

concept_tested: Comparing red and white muscle fibres in myoglobin content, oxidative capacity and the events they suit
stem: Red (dark) and white (pale) muscle fibres differ in their dependence on glycolysis. Which statement about them is correct?

options.A: White fibres contain more myoglobin and sustain aerobic oxidation, suiting endurance events such as marathon and swimming
options.B: Red fibres contain more myoglobin and sustain aerobic oxidation, suiting endurance events such as marathon and swimming
options.C: Red fibres accumulate lactate rapidly and fatigue quickly, suiting sprinting
options.D: White fibres contain more myoglobin yet fatigue quickly because they accumulate lactate

correct_answer_text: Red fibres contain more myoglobin and sustain aerobic oxidation, suiting endurance events such as marathon and swimming

distractor_rationale.A: The higher myoglobin content and the capacity for sustained aerobic oxidation belong to the red fibres, not the white ones.
distractor_rationale.C: Rapid lactate accumulation and quick fatigue are features of white fibres, which is why sprinters have a higher proportion of them.
distractor_rationale.D: White fibres do fatigue quickly through lactate accumulation, but they are the fibres with less myoglobin, which is why they are pale.

solution: Red (dark) fibres owe their colour to a higher myoglobin content and can sustain aerobic oxidation, which suits them to endurance events such as marathon running and swimming.
formula_principle: Red fibres are rich in myoglobin and sustain aerobic oxidation for endurance work; white fibres work rapidly and intensely, accumulate lactate and fatigue quickly.
common_misconception: Students link pale colour with oxygen-rich tissue, or transfer lactate accumulation and rapid fatigue to the red fibres.

concept_tested: Recall of the intracellular factors and the hormones that control the glycolytic rate
stem: The rate of glycolysis is stated to be controlled by an interplay of intracellular factors together with certain hormones. Which combination is correct?

options.A: ATP consumption, NADH2 regeneration and regulation of glycolytic enzymes, with glucagon, thyroxine and insulin
options.B: Oxygen availability and carbon dioxide removal, with glucagon, epinephrine and insulin
options.C: ATP consumption and regeneration of FADH2, with epinephrine, insulin and cortisol
options.D: ATP consumption, NADH2 regeneration and regulation of glycolytic enzymes, with glucagon, epinephrine and insulin

correct_answer_text: ATP consumption, NADH2 regeneration and regulation of glycolytic enzymes, with glucagon, epinephrine and insulin

distractor_rationale.A: The intracellular factors are right, but thyroxine is not among the hormones named as regulators of glycolysis.
distractor_rationale.B: Glycolysis itself neither uses oxygen nor releases carbon dioxide, so these gases are not given as controllers of its rate.
distractor_rationale.C: FADH2 is produced in the Krebs cycle and not in glycolysis, and cortisol is not named among the regulating hormones.

solution: Control of glycolysis rests on how fast ATP is consumed, how fast NADH2 is regenerated and how the glycolytic enzymes are regulated, with glucagon, epinephrine and insulin acting as hormonal regulators.
formula_principle: The glycolytic rate is controlled by the interplay between ATP consumption, NADH2 regeneration and regulation of glycolytic enzymes, and by the hormones glucagon, epinephrine and insulin.
common_misconception: Students assume that oxygen supply regulates glycolysis, although glycolysis proceeds identically whether or not oxygen is present.

concept_tested: Deriving ATP and NADH+H+ output when the pathway is entered at the triose stage instead of at glucose
stem: A cell-free preparation is supplied with glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate instead of glucose, and each molecule is carried through the remaining glycolytic reactions to pyruvic acid. Per glucose these reactions yield 4 ATP and 2 NADH+H+ from 2 such trioses. If 6 molecules of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate are supplied, how many ATP and NADH+H+ are formed, and how much ATP is invested?

options.A: 12 ATP and 6 NADH+H+, with 6 ATP invested
options.B: 6 ATP and 6 NADH+H+, with no ATP invested
options.C: 24 ATP and 12 NADH+H+, with no ATP invested
options.D: 12 ATP and 6 NADH+H+, with no ATP invested

correct_answer_text: 12 ATP and 6 NADH+H+, with no ATP invested

distractor_rationale.A: The two ATP-consuming steps lie in the preparatory phase, before glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate is formed, so they are bypassed entirely here.
distractor_rationale.B: This credits only one ATP to each triose, although each triose passes through two ATP-yielding conversions.
distractor_rationale.C: This treats each triose as if it were a whole glucose and so doubles both the ATP and the reduced coenzyme.

solution: Each glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate yields 2 ATP and 1 NADH+H+, so 6 of them give 12 ATP and 6 NADH+H+; because the two ATP-consuming phosphorylations happen before this intermediate is reached, no ATP is invested.
formula_principle: Per glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate: ATP = 4/2 = 2 and NADH+H+ = 2/2 = 1; the ATP investment of glycolysis occurs only in the preparatory phase, upstream of this triose.
common_misconception: Students carry the fixed two-ATP investment of glycolysis into any calculation, even when the pathway is entered below the steps that spend it.

concept_tested: Identifying the hydrogen acceptor and the product of lactic acid fermentation in muscle
stem: In skeletal muscle the NADH+H+ formed during glycolysis is reoxidised to NAD+ by donating one proton and two electrons to an acceptor. Which acceptor and which product are involved?

options.A: Acetaldehyde is the acceptor and ethanol is the product
options.B: Molecular oxygen is the acceptor and water is the product
options.C: Pyruvic acid is the acceptor and lactic acid is the product
options.D: Oxaloacetate is the acceptor and malate is the product

correct_answer_text: Pyruvic acid is the acceptor and lactic acid is the product

distractor_rationale.A: Acetaldehyde accepts hydrogen only in yeast, after pyruvate has first been decarboxylated; muscle does not carry out that decarboxylation.
distractor_rationale.B: Handing hydrogen to molecular oxygen to give water is terminal oxidation in aerobic respiration, which cannot occur in the absence of oxygen.
distractor_rationale.D: The malate to oxaloacetate conversion belongs to the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix and is not part of fermentation.

solution: In muscle the NADH+H+ from glycolysis reduces pyruvic acid to lactic acid, and the NAD+ released in the process becomes available for glycolysis again.
formula_principle: Lactic acid fermentation: 2 Pyruvic acid + 2 NADH+H+ --> 2 Lactic acid + 2 NAD+.
common_misconception: Students merge the two fermentations and expect muscle to pass hydrogen to acetaldehyde as yeast does.

options.C: Acetaldehyde is formed first and acetic acid finally

stem: Which difference between lactic acid fermentation in muscle and alcoholic fermentation in yeast is correct?

options.A: Carbon dioxide is released in alcoholic fermentation but not in lactic acid fermentation
options.B: Carbon dioxide is released in lactic acid fermentation but not in alcoholic fermentation
options.C: NADH+H+ is reoxidised in lactic acid fermentation but not in alcoholic fermentation
options.D: Pyruvic acid is the starting compound in alcoholic fermentation but not in lactic acid fermentation

common_misconception: Students assume carbon dioxide is released in every form of respiration, including the reduction of pyruvic acid to lactic acid.

concept_tested: Recognising that the oxidation of NADH+H+ in fermentation serves coenzyme regeneration and not ATP synthesis
stem: In respiration, oxidation of NADH+H+ through the electron transport system yields ATP. In fermentation the NADH+H+ formed during glycolysis is also oxidised. What is the purpose of this oxidation in fermentation?

options.A: Regeneration of NAD+ so that glycolysis can continue, with no ATP formed at this step
options.B: Production of three ATP for each NADH+H+, as in the electron transport system
options.C: Production of water by handing the hydrogen to molecular oxygen
options.D: Complete oxidation of pyruvic acid to carbon dioxide

correct_answer_text: Regeneration of NAD+ so that glycolysis can continue, with no ATP formed at this step

distractor_rationale.B: That conversion belongs to oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane, which does not operate when oxygen is absent.
distractor_rationale.C: Formation of metabolic water is terminal oxidation of aerobic respiration and requires the molecular oxygen that fermentation lacks.
distractor_rationale.D: Pyruvic acid is reduced rather than oxidised in fermentation, and its carbon is retained in lactic acid or ethanol.

solution: Fermentation oxidises NADH+H+ only to return NAD+ to glycolysis; because the hydrogen goes to pyruvic acid or acetaldehyde and not into the electron transport system, no ATP is formed at this step.
formula_principle: In fermentation the reduced coenzyme is reoxidised by an organic acceptor, which regenerates NAD+ for glycolysis but is not coupled to phosphorylation of ADP.
common_misconception: Students apply the balance sheet value of three ATP per NADH+H+ to every oxidation of the coenzyme, including the one that happens anaerobically.

concept_tested: Determining the net ATP gain per glucose when only the glycolytic reactions yield ATP
stem: During fermentation of one glucose molecule, ATP is formed only in the reactions of glycolysis, where 4 ATP are produced and 2 are consumed, and the subsequent conversion of pyruvic acid yields no ATP. What is the net ATP gain per glucose?

distractor_rationale.A: This is the gross output of the pay-off phase and ignores the 2 ATP invested in the preparatory phase.
distractor_rationale.C: This adds the ATP that the balance sheet credits to oxidative phosphorylation of the glycolytic NADH+H+, which cannot occur without oxygen.
distractor_rationale.D: 8 is the net benefit entered for glycolysis in the aerobic balance sheet, which already credits oxidative phosphorylation of the two NADH+H+.

solution: Only the substrate-level phosphorylations of glycolysis yield ATP in fermentation, so the net gain is 4 - 2 = 2 ATP per glucose.
formula_principle: Net ATP in fermentation = ATP produced in glycolysis (4) - ATP consumed in glycolysis (2), since the conversion of pyruvic acid contributes none.
common_misconception: Students transfer the aerobic net benefit of the glycolysis row to fermentation, forgetting that the NADH+H+ is spent on reducing pyruvic acid instead of being oxidised through the electron transport system.

concept_tested: Scaling net ATP and carbon dioxide output of alcoholic fermentation to several glucose molecules
stem: Yeast ferments 4 molecules of glucose to ethanol in the absence of oxygen. Glycolysis produces 4 ATP and consumes 2 ATP per glucose, and each of the two pyruvic acid molecules formed per glucose loses one carbon dioxide during alcoholic fermentation. How many net ATP and how many carbon dioxide molecules are formed?

distractor_rationale.B: This uses the gross figure of 4 ATP per glucose without subtracting the 2 ATP invested.
distractor_rationale.C: This releases one carbon dioxide per glucose, forgetting that each glucose gives two pyruvic acid molecules and each loses a carbon.
distractor_rationale.D: This assumes the carbon skeleton of pyruvic acid is fully oxidised to three carbon dioxide molecules, which happens only in aerobic respiration.

concept_tested: Explaining why anaerobic respiration releases far less energy per glucose than aerobic respiration
stem: Why is much less energy obtained per glucose molecule in anaerobic respiration than in aerobic respiration?

options.A: Glucose is completely oxidised, but the ATP that is formed is at once hydrolysed back to ADP
options.B: Glucose is not completely oxidised, and the reduced coenzyme is spent on lactic acid or ethanol
options.C: Fewer glucose molecules are able to enter glycolysis when oxygen is absent, so fewer ATP are formed
options.D: Anaerobic respiration omits glycolysis altogether and begins at the conversion of pyruvic acid

correct_answer_text: Glucose is not completely oxidised, and the reduced coenzyme is spent on lactic acid or ethanol

distractor_rationale.A: Fermentation leaves the carbon of glucose locked in lactic acid or ethanol, so the oxidation is incomplete, and no such wholesale hydrolysis of the ATP formed is described.
distractor_rationale.C: The shortfall is in ATP obtained per glucose, not in the number of glucose molecules entering the pathway; glycolysis proceeds identically either way.
distractor_rationale.D: Glycolysis is common to both, and anaerobic respiration consists of glycolysis followed by the conversion of pyruvic acid to lactic acid or ethanol.

solution: In fermentation the carbon of glucose is retained in lactic acid or ethanol instead of being fully oxidised, and the NADH+H+ of glycolysis is used to reduce pyruvic acid rather than being oxidised through the electron transport system, so only the substrate-level phosphorylations of glycolysis contribute ATP.
formula_principle: Anaerobic respiration stops at lactic acid or ethanol, so the substrate is only partly oxidised and the reduced coenzymes are not passed to the electron transport system for oxidative phosphorylation.
common_misconception: Students explain the lower anaerobic yield by supposing that the pathway is shorter because glycolysis is skipped, rather than because the oxidation is incomplete.
difficulty_basis: Extended synthesis across several claims, stages or calculations with high working-memory and trap density

subtopic: Try this: germinating seeds in mercury
concept_tested: Interpreting the mercury and potassium hydroxide activity on germinating seeds
stem: Seed coats are removed from a few germinating peas, which are placed in a test tube filled with mercury; the tube is inverted in a trough of mercury. As germination proceeds a gas collects at the top of the tube, and when a pellet of potassium hydroxide is introduced it rises to the top, absorbs the gas and the mercury fills the tube again. What does the activity establish?

options.A: The gas is oxygen, and the seeds release oxygen as they germinate
options.B: The gas is carbon dioxide, and the seeds respire anaerobically in the absence of oxygen
options.C: The gas is carbon dioxide, and the seeds respire aerobically using oxygen dissolved in the mercury
options.D: The gas is water vapour, which the potassium hydroxide takes up on condensation

correct_answer_text: The gas is carbon dioxide, and the seeds respire anaerobically in the absence of oxygen

distractor_rationale.A: Potassium hydroxide absorbs carbon dioxide and not oxygen, and germinating seeds do not evolve oxygen.
distractor_rationale.C: The mercury seals the seeds off from air, so no oxygen is available and the respiration demonstrated is anaerobic.
distractor_rationale.D: The gas collected is a product of respiration that potassium hydroxide absorbs chemically; water vapour is not what the activity is designed to show.

solution: The gas that collects is carbon dioxide, shown by its complete absorption by the potassium hydroxide pellet, and because the mercury excludes air the seeds must have produced it by respiring anaerobically.
formula_principle: Potassium hydroxide absorbs carbon dioxide; evolution of carbon dioxide by seeds sealed under mercury, where no oxygen is available, demonstrates anaerobic respiration.
common_misconception: Students assume that any respiring tissue must be taking in oxygen and so read the setup as a demonstration of aerobic respiration.

subtopic: Nature of the connecting link reaction
concept_tested: Naming the reaction type by which pyruvic acid becomes acetyl CoA
stem: Pyruvic acid formed at the end of glycolysis is converted into acetyl CoA in the step that connects glycolysis with the Krebs cycle. This step removes carbon dioxide and hydrogen from the substrate. What type of reaction is this?

distractor_rationale.B: Substrate level phosphorylation is the direct transfer of a phosphate group from a substrate to ADP; no phosphate is transferred when pyruvic acid becomes acetyl CoA.
distractor_rationale.C: Oxidative phosphorylation is the phosphorylation of ADP using energy from the oxidation of NADH+H+ and FADH2 on the inner mitochondrial membrane, not a reaction of the substrate itself.
distractor_rationale.D: Condensation is the joining of two molecules with loss of a small molecule, which is what happens when acetyl CoA meets oxaloacetate, not when pyruvic acid is broken down.

solution: The step is described as the connecting link reaction between glycolysis and the Krebs cycle, and its reaction type is oxidative decarboxylation because oxidation and loss of carbon dioxide occur together.
formula_principle: The conversion of pyruvic acid to acetyl CoA is an oxidative decarboxylation: hydrogen is removed by oxidation and a carbon is removed as carbon dioxide in the same step.
common_misconception: Students hear the word oxidative and reach for oxidative phosphorylation, which is an ATP-forming process on the inner membrane, not a substrate reaction.
difficulty_basis: One-step recognition or direct use of a single prescribed fact; low reasoning and distractor load

concept_tested: Listing all three products formed when one pyruvic acid is converted to acetyl CoA
stem: One molecule of pyruvic acid is completely converted in the connecting link reaction. Which set names all the products of that single conversion?

options.A: Acetyl CoA, carbon dioxide and FADH2
options.B: Acetyl CoA, carbon dioxide and ATP
options.D: Acetyl CoA, carbon dioxide and NADH+H+

correct_answer_text: Acetyl CoA, carbon dioxide and NADH+H+

distractor_rationale.B: No ATP is generated in this step; the energy of the oxidation is carried away as reduced coenzyme rather than as a phosphate bond.

formula_principle: The connecting link reaction converts pyruvic acid plus NAD+ plus CoA-SH into acetyl CoA, carbon dioxide and NADH+H+.

subtopic: Enzyme and coenzymes of the link reaction
concept_tested: Matching the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex with the coenzymes it uses
stem: Which combination of enzyme and coenzymes carries out the conversion of pyruvic acid to acetyl CoA?

options.A: Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, with FAD+ and CoA-SH
options.B: Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, with NAD+ and CoA-SH
options.C: Citrate synthase, with NAD+ and CoA-SH
options.D: Isocitrate dehydrogenase, with NAD+ and FAD+

correct_answer_text: Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, with NAD+ and CoA-SH

distractor_rationale.A: The enzyme is right but the hydrogen acceptor is wrong; this step reduces NAD+ to NADH+H+, and FAD+ is not a coenzyme of the link reaction.
distractor_rationale.C: Citrate synthase acts one step later, joining acetyl CoA to oxaloacetate, and it releases CoA-SH rather than oxidising pyruvic acid.
distractor_rationale.D: Isocitrate dehydrogenase works inside the Krebs cycle on isocitrate, and it uses NAD+ alone rather than a pair of hydrogen acceptors.

solution: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex oxidises pyruvic acid, passing hydrogen to NAD+, and transfers the resulting acetyl group to CoA-SH, so both NAD+ and CoA-SH are required.

subtopic: Site of the connecting link reaction
concept_tested: Contrasting the cellular location of the link reaction in eukaryotes and in prokaryotes
stem: Where does the conversion of pyruvic acid to acetyl CoA take place in a eukaryotic cell, and where does the same conversion take place in a prokaryotic cell?

options.A: In the cytosol in eukaryotes and in the mitochondria in prokaryotes
options.B: In the mitochondria in eukaryotes and in the cytosol in prokaryotes
options.C: In the mitochondria in eukaryotes and in the mitochondria in prokaryotes
options.D: In the cytosol in eukaryotes and in the cytosol in prokaryotes

correct_answer_text: In the mitochondria in eukaryotes and in the cytosol in prokaryotes

distractor_rationale.C: Prokaryotic cells lack mitochondria, so the same compartment cannot serve both cell types for this reaction.

formula_principle: The conversion of pyruvic acid to acetyl CoA occurs in the mitochondria in eukaryotes and in the cytosol in prokaryotes.
common_misconception: Students assume every stage after glycolysis must be mitochondrial in all cells, and so give the same answer for prokaryotes.

subtopic: Vitamin requirement of the link reaction
concept_tested: Predicting the immediate metabolic consequence of a thiamin deficiency
stem: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex cannot function in the absence of thiamin (vitamin B1). A person's diet is severely deficient in thiamin. Which immediate consequence for the connecting link reaction follows?

options.A: Pyruvic acid is converted into acetyl CoA without release of carbon dioxide
options.B: Acetyl CoA is formed but no NADH+H+ accompanies its formation
options.C: Pyruvic acid enters the Krebs cycle directly in place of acetyl CoA
options.D: Pyruvic acid can no longer be converted into acetyl CoA

correct_answer_text: Pyruvic acid can no longer be converted into acetyl CoA

distractor_rationale.B: The reduction of NAD+ is carried out by the same complex, so a deficiency that blocks the complex blocks the whole conversion rather than one of its outputs.
distractor_rationale.C: Only acetyl CoA condenses with oxaloacetate to start the cycle; pyruvic acid has no route into the cycle that bypasses this step.

formula_principle: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex requires thiamin (vitamin B1) as a coenzyme, so a thiamin deficiency disables the whole connecting link reaction.
common_misconception: Students treat the vitamin as affecting only one output of the reaction, such as the carbon dioxide or the reduced coenzyme, instead of the whole catalysed conversion.

subtopic: ATP accounting for the link reaction
concept_tested: Computing the ATP contributed by the connecting link reaction for one glucose
stem: One glucose molecule yields two molecules of pyruvic acid, and each of them undergoes the connecting link reaction, producing one NADH+H+ each. Using the prescribed MHT-CET textbook balance sheet each NADH+H+ is worth 3 ATP, and this step consumes no ATP. How many ATP does the connecting link reaction contribute per glucose?

distractor_rationale.A: This counts only one pyruvic acid; each glucose gives two pyruvic acid molecules, so the link reaction runs twice per glucose.
distractor_rationale.B: This counts the two NADH+H+ molecules themselves rather than converting each of them into 3 ATP.
distractor_rationale.D: This applies a value of 2 ATP per reduced coenzyme, which is the figure for FADH2; the link reaction produces NADH+H+, worth 3 ATP each.

solution: Two pyruvic acid molecules each give one NADH+H+, so 2 NADH+H+ are formed. At 3 ATP per NADH+H+ this is 2 x 3 = 6 ATP, and nothing is consumed at this step, so the net contribution is 6 ATP.
formula_principle: ATP from the link reaction per glucose = (number of pyruvic acid molecules) x (NADH+H+ per pyruvic acid) x (ATP per NADH+H+).
common_misconception: Students forget that glycolysis delivers two pyruvic acid molecules per glucose and therefore halve every quantity that belongs to this step.

concept_tested: Identifying the acceptor molecule that acetyl CoA condenses with
stem: Acetyl CoA entering the Krebs cycle condenses with the acceptor molecule of the cycle, in a reaction catalysed by citrate synthase in which CoA-SH is released. With which compound does acetyl CoA condense?

distractor_rationale.A: Alpha-ketoglutarate is formed later in the cycle and is itself oxidatively decarboxylated; it does not accept the incoming acetyl group.

distractor_rationale.D: Malate is the compound oxidised in the last step of the cycle, and its product rather than malate itself accepts the acetyl group.

subtopic: Order of intermediates in the first half
concept_tested: Ordering citrate, cis-aconitate, isocitrate and oxalosuccinic acid as printed
stem: Arrange the following species of the Krebs cycle in the order in which they appear in the prescribed pathway sequence: citrate, cis-aconitate, isocitrate, oxalosuccinic acid.

distractor_rationale.B: This swaps the dehydration and hydration products; citrate first loses water to give cis-aconitate, which then takes up water to give isocitrate.

distractor_rationale.D: Oxalosuccinic acid is formed from isocitrate during its oxidative decarboxylation, so it cannot come before isocitrate.

subtopic: Substrate level phosphorylation in the cycle
concept_tested: Identifying the single step of the Krebs cycle that forms GTP or ATP directly
stem: Exactly one step of the Krebs cycle produces GTP (ATP) by substrate level phosphorylation. Which conversion is it?

distractor_rationale.A: This step is an oxidative decarboxylation that yields NADH+H+ and carbon dioxide; the phosphate-forming energy is still locked in the thioester bond of succinyl-CoA.
distractor_rationale.B: This is a dehydrogenation in which FAD+ is reduced to FADH2; no phosphate group is transferred to ADP.
distractor_rationale.C: This is a hydration catalysed by fumarase, involving neither oxidation nor phosphorylation.

common_misconception: Students associate the ATP of the cycle with one of the dehydrogenation steps because those visibly release energy, and so pick succinate to fumarate.

concept_tested: Identifying the two conversions of the cycle that release carbon dioxide
stem: Carbon dioxide is released at exactly two conversions within one turn of the Krebs cycle. Which pair of conversions are these?

options.B: Isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate and alpha-ketoglutarate to succinyl-CoA
options.C: Succinate to fumarate and fumarate to malate

concept_tested: Computing the total ATP attributable to a single turn of the Krebs cycle
stem: One turn of the Krebs cycle yields 3 NADH+H+, 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP counted as 1 ATP. Using the prescribed MHT-CET balance-sheet convention of 3 ATP per NADH+H+ and 2 ATP per FADH2, how many ATP are attributable to one turn?

distractor_rationale.A: This omits the GTP formed by substrate level phosphorylation and counts only the reduced coenzymes.
distractor_rationale.B: This applies 2 ATP to every reduced coenzyme, whereas only FADH2 is worth 2 ATP and each NADH+H+ is worth 3.
distractor_rationale.C: This is the figure for two turns, that is for a whole glucose, rather than for a single turn.

solution: The three NADH+H+ give 3 x 3 = 9 ATP, the single FADH2 gives 1 x 2 = 2 ATP, and the GTP counts as 1 ATP. The total for one turn is 9 + 2 + 1 = 12 ATP.
formula_principle: ATP per turn = (NADH+H+ per turn x 3) + (FADH2 per turn x 2) + (GTP per turn counted as ATP).
common_misconception: Students apply a single conversion factor to all reduced coenzymes, or quietly drop the GTP because it is not called ATP in the diagram.
difficulty_basis: Multi-part interpretation, pathway reasoning or calculation linking several facts with plausible traps

concept_tested: Computing the carbon dioxide released by the Krebs cycle per glucose

distractor_rationale.A: This counts a single turn only; a glucose molecule gives two acetyl CoA and therefore drives two turns.

subtopic: Split of the Krebs contribution by mechanism
concept_tested: Separating the oxidative phosphorylation share from the substrate level share of the cycle
stem: The Krebs cycle contributes a total of 24 ATP for every glucose molecule oxidised. Of the mechanisms involved, substrate level phosphorylation supplies 1 GTP counted as 1 ATP in each turn, and two turns occur per glucose. How many of the 24 ATP arise by oxidative phosphorylation?

distractor_rationale.A: This subtracts the GTP of a single turn; two turns occur per glucose, so 2 ATP come from substrate level phosphorylation.
distractor_rationale.B: This subtracts four rather than two, treating each turn as though it carried out two substrate level phosphorylations.

subtopic: Reduced coenzyme yield of the cycle
concept_tested: Counting the reduced coenzyme molecules delivered by the cycle per glucose
stem: Each turn of the Krebs cycle produces 3 NADH+H+ and 1 FADH2, and two turns occur for every glucose molecule oxidised. How many molecules of reduced coenzyme in total does the Krebs cycle deliver per glucose?

distractor_rationale.C: This adds the two NADH+H+ of glycolysis, which are produced in the cytoplasm and not by the Krebs cycle.

concept_tested: Tracking the six carbon atoms of glucose into carbon dioxide
stem: One glucose molecule of six carbon atoms is split by glycolysis into two molecules of pyruvic acid of three carbon atoms each. Each pyruvic acid then loses one carbon as carbon dioxide in the connecting link reaction, and each of the two turns of the Krebs cycle releases two more molecules of carbon dioxide. How many of the six carbon atoms of the glucose have left as carbon dioxide once both stages are complete?

distractor_rationale.A: This counts only the carbon released by the two turns of the cycle and ignores the two carbon atoms lost in the connecting link reaction.
distractor_rationale.B: This counts only the connecting link reaction and leaves the four carbon atoms released within the cycle unaccounted for.
distractor_rationale.D: This follows a single pyruvic acid through to completion and forgets that glycolysis produces two of them per glucose.

solution: The two connecting link reactions release 2 molecules of carbon dioxide and the two turns of the cycle release 2 x 2 = 4 more, giving 6 in all. That equals the six carbon atoms of one glucose, so all of the carbon of the glucose has been released.
formula_principle: Total carbon dioxide per glucose = (carbon dioxide from the two link reactions) + (carbon dioxide per turn x turns per glucose), and this must equal the carbon content of the glucose.
common_misconception: Students stop at the four carbon dioxide molecules of the cycle and conclude that some carbon of the glucose is never released.

subtopic: Substrate level phosphorylation across the pathway
concept_tested: Totalling the ATP made by direct phosphate transfer during aerobic oxidation of one glucose
stem: In the aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule, substrate level phosphorylation produces 4 ATP during glycolysis and 1 GTP counted as 1 ATP in each turn of the Krebs cycle, with two turns occurring per glucose. The connecting link reaction contributes none. What is the total ATP produced by substrate level phosphorylation?

distractor_rationale.B: This counts the GTP of one turn only, although two turns of the cycle run for every glucose molecule.
distractor_rationale.C: This is the glycolytic contribution alone and omits the GTP of the Krebs cycle turns.
distractor_rationale.D: This is the net gain of glycolysis after the two ATP invested in the preparatory phase, not the amount produced by direct phosphate transfer.

solution: Glycolysis contributes 4 ATP by direct phosphate transfer and the Krebs cycle contributes 1 x 2 = 2, giving 4 + 2 = 6 ATP by substrate level phosphorylation for one glucose.
formula_principle: Total substrate level phosphorylation = (ATP so formed in glycolysis) + (GTP or ATP per turn x turns per glucose).
common_misconception: Students report the net glycolytic gain of 2 instead of the 4 actually produced, because they subtract the investment before totalling.

subtopic: Working back from a measured ATP total
concept_tested: Deducing the number of turns and the carbon dioxide released from an ATP figure
stem: A preparation of mitochondria is supplied with acetyl CoA and yields 60 ATP from Krebs cycle turns alone. Each turn gives 3 NADH+H+, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP counted as 1 ATP, and 2 molecules of carbon dioxide. Each NADH+H+ is worth 3 ATP and each FADH2 is worth 2 ATP. How many turns occurred, and how much carbon dioxide was released?

options.A: 5 turns and 5 molecules of carbon dioxide
options.B: 5 turns and 10 molecules of carbon dioxide
options.C: 6 turns and 12 molecules of carbon dioxide
options.D: 10 turns and 20 molecules of carbon dioxide

correct_answer_text: 5 turns and 10 molecules of carbon dioxide

distractor_rationale.A: The number of turns is right but each turn releases two molecules of carbon dioxide, not one.
distractor_rationale.C: This takes each turn to be worth 10 ATP, which follows from valuing every reduced coenzyme at 2 ATP and dropping the GTP.
distractor_rationale.D: This values each turn at 6 ATP, counting the reduced coenzymes as single ATP molecules rather than applying the stated conversion factors.

solution: One turn yields 9 + 2 + 1 = 12 ATP, so 60 ATP corresponds to 60 / 12 = 5 turns. Each turn releases 2 molecules of carbon dioxide, so 5 x 2 = 10 molecules were released.
formula_principle: Turns = (total ATP) divided by (ATP per turn), where ATP per turn = 3 x 3 + 1 x 2 + 1; carbon dioxide = turns x 2.
common_misconception: Students value all reduced coenzymes alike or omit the GTP, which changes the ATP per turn and so gives the wrong number of turns.

subtopic: Hydrogen acceptor at the oxidation steps
concept_tested: Finding the single oxidation of the cycle that does not use NAD+
stem: Rule: in the Krebs cycle the oxidation steps are catalysed by dehydrogenases, and these hand the removed hydrogen to NAD+ to form NADH+H+. Exactly one oxidation of the cycle departs from this pattern. Which conversion is it?

distractor_rationale.B: This oxidation follows the rule; isocitrate dehydrogenase reduces NAD+ and also releases carbon dioxide.
distractor_rationale.C: Malate dehydrogenase also reduces NAD+, so this closing oxidation conforms to the pattern rather than breaking it.
distractor_rationale.D: The alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex reduces NAD+ as well, with CoA-SH taken up and carbon dioxide released.

solution: Succinate dehydrogenase is the one enzyme of the cycle that passes hydrogen to FAD+, giving FADH2. This is why one turn produces 3 NADH+H+ but only 1 FADH2.
formula_principle: Three of the four oxidations of the cycle reduce NAD+ to NADH+H+, while succinate dehydrogenase reduces FAD+ to FADH2.
common_misconception: Students generalise from the three NAD+ steps and treat every dehydrogenation of the cycle as NAD+ dependent, which then makes their ATP arithmetic too high.

subtopic: An enzyme acting twice in one turn
concept_tested: Recognising the enzyme that catalyses two consecutive conversions
stem: Rule: in the Krebs cycle most named enzymes catalyse a single conversion of the turn. Which of the following enzymes departs from that pattern by catalysing two consecutive conversions?

distractor_rationale.A: Citrate synthase acts once, joining acetyl CoA to oxaloacetate to give citrate, and takes no part in the conversions that follow.
distractor_rationale.B: Fumarase acts once, adding water to fumarate to give malate, and it does not catalyse the oxidation that follows.
distractor_rationale.C: Malate dehydrogenase acts once, oxidising malate to oxaloacetate at the close of the turn.

solution: The conversion of citrate to isocitrate is shown as two steps through cis-aconitate, and the same enzyme, aconitase, catalyses both the removal of water and its addition.
formula_principle: Aconitase catalyses both the dehydration of citrate to cis-aconitate and the hydration of cis-aconitate to isocitrate.
common_misconception: Students who learn a shortened cycle in which citrate goes directly to isocitrate never see the two aconitase steps and assume one enzyme per conversion throughout.

stem: Four oxidation steps of the Krebs cycle are catalysed by dehydrogenases. Which of the following named enzymes of the cycle instead catalyses a hydration?

distractor_rationale.B: This enzyme carries out one of the four oxidations, removing hydrogen from succinate and reducing FAD+.

subtopic: Order of intermediates across the whole cycle
concept_tested: Ordering four widely separated species of the cycle as printed
stem: Arrange the following species in the order in which they appear in one turn of the Krebs cycle in the prescribed sequence: alpha-ketoglutarate, cis-aconitate, malate, succinyl-CoA.

distractor_rationale.A: This places succinyl-CoA before alpha-ketoglutarate, whereas succinyl-CoA is formed by the oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-ketoglutarate.
distractor_rationale.B: cis-Aconitate belongs to the first half of the turn, between citrate and isocitrate, so it precedes alpha-ketoglutarate.
distractor_rationale.D: Malate lies near the close of the turn, after succinate and fumarate, so it cannot precede succinyl-CoA.

solution: cis-Aconitate lies early, between citrate and isocitrate. Alpha-ketoglutarate follows oxalosuccinic acid, succinyl-CoA follows alpha-ketoglutarate, and malate lies late, between fumarate and oxaloacetate.
formula_principle: The full printed order of one turn is citrate, cis-aconitate, isocitrate, oxalosuccinic acid, alpha-ketoglutarate, succinyl-CoA, succinate, fumarate, malate, oxaloacetate.
common_misconception: Students who cannot place cis-aconitate at all default to putting the familiar names first and the unfamiliar name last.

concept_tested: Explaining why oxaloacetate is not consumed overall despite being used at the first step
stem: Rule: a compound that is used up at the first step of a metabolic sequence has to be supplied continuously from outside that sequence. Oxaloacetate is used up at the first step of the Krebs cycle, yet the cycle can keep running without an outside supply of it. Which feature of the cycle accounts for this?

options.A: It is formed from acetyl CoA during the opening condensation step
options.B: It is produced from pyruvic acid by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex
options.C: It is re-formed at the last step of the same turn by the oxidation of malate
options.D: It is released along with carbon dioxide at the oxidative decarboxylation steps

correct_answer_text: It is re-formed at the last step of the same turn by the oxidation of malate

distractor_rationale.A: The condensation consumes both acetyl CoA and oxaloacetate to make citrate; it cannot also produce the oxaloacetate it uses.
distractor_rationale.B: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex produces acetyl CoA, not oxaloacetate, so this reaction cannot replenish the acceptor.
distractor_rationale.D: Those steps yield alpha-ketoglutarate and succinyl-CoA together with carbon dioxide and NADH+H+, and neither of them yields oxaloacetate.

solution: Because malate dehydrogenase restores oxaloacetate at the end of every turn, the same molecule can accept the next acetyl CoA. This regeneration is what makes the pathway a cycle rather than a linear sequence.
formula_principle: Oxaloacetate is consumed in the opening condensation and regenerated in the final dehydrogenation of malate, so there is no net consumption of it in a turn.
common_misconception: Students treat oxaloacetate as an ordinary substrate that must be steadily supplied, and so cannot explain how the cycle sustains itself.
difficulty_basis: Multi-part interpretation, pathway reasoning or calculation linking several facts with plausible traps

concept_tested: Defining the term amphibolic as applied to the Krebs cycle
stem: The Krebs cycle is described as an amphibolic pathway. What does this term mean?

options.A: A pathway involving only the oxidative breakdown of substrates
options.B: A pathway involving catabolism as well as anabolism
options.C: A pathway involving only the building up of complex molecules
options.D: A pathway that can operate both in the cytoplasm and in the mitochondria

correct_answer_text: A pathway involving catabolism as well as anabolism

distractor_rationale.A: That describes a purely catabolic pathway, which is exactly the description the chapter says is not entirely correct for the Krebs cycle.
distractor_rationale.C: That describes a purely anabolic pathway; the Krebs cycle plainly also oxidises the acetyl part of acetyl CoA and releases carbon dioxide.
distractor_rationale.D: The term refers to the chemistry of the pathway rather than to its location, and the reactions of the cycle are confined to the mitochondrial matrix.

solution: The Krebs cycle oxidises the acetyl part of acetyl CoA with release of energy and carbon dioxide, and at the same time supplies intermediates that are used as precursors for synthesis, so it is both catabolic and anabolic.
formula_principle: An amphibolic pathway is one that involves catabolism as well as anabolism.

concept_tested: Naming the single compound through which amino acids and fatty acids join the cycle
stem: Amino acids from protein metabolism and fatty acids from lipid metabolism also take part in the Krebs cycle. Through which compound do they enter it?

distractor_rationale.A: Oxaloacetate is the acceptor already present in the cycle and is named as a precursor for aspartic acid, not as the port of entry for these substrates.

concept_tested: Deciding which named step of aerobic respiration is bypassed when fatty acids are respired
stem: Aerobic respiration is described as operating through glycolysis, production of acetyl CoA, the Krebs cycle, the electron transfer chain reaction and terminal oxidation. Fatty acids join the pathway as acetyl CoA. Which of these named steps is omitted when fatty acids are used as the respiratory substrate?

distractor_rationale.B: The Krebs cycle is precisely the stage that fatty acid derived acetyl CoA feeds into, so it is the one stage that certainly still runs.
distractor_rationale.C: The reduced coenzymes produced from fatty acid oxidation still have to be oxidised, so the electron transfer chain is still needed.

subtopic: Why respiration is not purely catabolic
concept_tested: Identifying the observation that breaks a purely catabolic description of the Krebs cycle
stem: Rule: a pathway that oxidises its substrates stepwise, releases energy and gives off carbon dioxide is a catabolic pathway. The Krebs cycle does all of these things, yet the prescribed account states calling it catabolic is not entirely correct. Which observation makes it an exception to the rule?

options.A: It regenerates oxidised coenzymes that are used again in later turns
options.B: It releases its energy in many small steps instead of all at once
options.C: It accepts substrates derived from carbohydrates, fats and proteins alike
options.D: Some of its intermediates are withdrawn as precursors for the synthesis of other biomolecules

correct_answer_text: Some of its intermediates are withdrawn as precursors for the synthesis of other biomolecules

distractor_rationale.A: Regeneration of coenzymes is part of the oxidative machinery itself and does not amount to the building up of new biomolecules.
distractor_rationale.B: Stepwise release is a feature of how catabolism is organised and does not make the pathway anabolic in any part.
distractor_rationale.C: That makes it a common oxidative pathway, but every one of those substrates is still being broken down rather than built up.

solution: Acetyl CoA and intermediates such as alpha-ketoglutarate and oxaloacetate are drawn off as needed for the synthesis of fatty acids, glutamic acid and aspartic acid. Because synthesis as well as breakdown depends on the cycle, it is correctly called amphibolic.
formula_principle: A pathway is amphibolic when its reactions serve anabolism as well as catabolism; withdrawal of intermediates as precursors for synthesis is the anabolic contribution of the Krebs cycle.
common_misconception: Students take breadth of substrates, or stepwise energy release, as the reason for the amphibolic label, since both are prominent features of the pathway.

concept_tested: Reasoning out why heavy withdrawal of intermediates limits the oxidative output of the cycle
stem: A cell is rapidly synthesising glutamic acid and aspartic acid, and so withdraws large amounts of alpha-ketoglutarate and oxaloacetate from the Krebs cycle. The supply of acetyl CoA to the cell is unchanged. Which statement best explains why the oxidative output of the cycle nevertheless falls?

options.A: Alpha-ketoglutarate carries the acetyl group through the cycle, so its removal leaves the acetyl group with no carrier
options.B: Both intermediates act as hydrogen acceptors at the oxidation steps, so their removal leaves the dehydrogenases without acceptors
options.C: Both intermediates supply the CoA-SH needed at the condensation step, so their removal blocks the formation of citrate
options.D: Oxaloacetate must be present at the start of each turn to accept acetyl CoA, so its removal limits the number of turns

correct_answer_text: Oxaloacetate must be present at the start of each turn to accept acetyl CoA, so its removal limits the number of turns

distractor_rationale.A: The acetyl group is carried into the cycle by coenzyme A and is handed to oxaloacetate at the condensation step; alpha-ketoglutarate has no such carrying role.
distractor_rationale.B: The hydrogen acceptors at those steps are NAD+ and FAD+, not the acids of the cycle themselves.
distractor_rationale.C: CoA-SH is released at the condensation step rather than being supplied by the intermediates of the cycle.

solution: Every turn begins with the condensation of acetyl CoA with oxaloacetate and ends with the regeneration of oxaloacetate from malate. If oxaloacetate is drawn off for aspartic acid synthesis, fewer molecules are left to accept acetyl CoA, so fewer turns occur and less reduced coenzyme and carbon dioxide are produced even though acetyl CoA is plentiful.
formula_principle: The cycle can turn only as often as oxaloacetate is available to condense with acetyl CoA, so anabolic withdrawal of intermediates competes with the oxidative role of the pathway.
common_misconception: Students treat the anabolic and catabolic roles of the cycle as independent, and do not see that withdrawing an intermediate removes the acceptor that the next turn depends on.

subtopic: Site of the electron transport system
concept_tested: Membrane on which the electron carriers of the electron transport system are arranged
stem: The electron carriers and enzymes that oxidise the NADH+H+ and FADH2 produced during glycolysis, the connecting link reaction and the Krebs cycle are arranged in the form of complexes. On which part of the mitochondrion are they arranged?

options.B: Outer chamber of the mitochondrion — ETC location

distractor_rationale.A: The matrix houses the reactions of the Krebs cycle; the carriers of the transport system are embedded in the inner membrane rather than dissolved in the matrix.

III: The same pathway can supply intermediates used in the synthesis of other biomolecules such as amino acids. IV: The many steps allow the pathway to continue without enzymes once it has begun. Which statements are among the purposes served by such stepwise metabolism?

distractor_rationale.A: This omits the supply of intermediates for the synthesis of other biomolecules, which is one of the stated purposes.
distractor_rationale.B: This admits the claim that the pathway can run without enzymes, whereas each step needs its own enzyme, and it drops the improved capture of bond energy.
distractor_rationale.D: This admits the enzyme-free claim and drops the regulation of rate and energy output, which is one of the stated purposes.

solution: Better capture of the chemical bond energy as ATP, regulation of the rate and energy output through the enzymes of the individual steps, and supply of intermediates for the synthesis of other biomolecules are the purposes served; a pathway cannot proceed without its enzymes, since it is those enzymes that make regulation possible.
formula_principle: The three stated purposes of stepwise metabolism are better capture of bond energy as ATP, regulation of pathway rate and energy output through the enzymes of the individual steps, and provision of intermediates for biosynthesis.
common_misconception: Students read the many steps as a self-sustaining chain reaction and accept the claim that the pathway can carry on once started without enzymes.

concept_tested: Calculating and interpreting respiratory quotient
stem: A respiring tissue consumes 50 ml of oxygen and releases 35 ml of carbon dioxide in the same interval. What is its respiratory quotient and the most likely main substrate?

distractor_rationale.A: 1.0; carbohydrate is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required calculating and interpreting respiratory quotient and therefore cannot be the single correct response.
distractor_rationale.B: 0.5; organic acid is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required calculating and interpreting respiratory quotient and therefore cannot be the single correct response.

distractor_rationale.C: This places the rectum before the jejunum; the jejunum is a part of the small intestine and is reached long before the rectum.
distractor_rationale.D: This places the jejunum before the pyloric sphincter; material can reach the small intestine only after passing the pyloric sphincter.

solution: The capsule passes the cardiac sphincter at the junction of the oesophagus and stomach, then the pyloric sphincter guarding the exit of the stomach into the duodenum, then travels through the jejunum, and finally reaches the rectum.
formula_principle: Sequence along the alimentary canal, including the two sphincters of the stomach: cardiac sphincter, pyloric sphincter, jejunum, rectum.
common_misconception: Students attach the cardiac sphincter to the exit of the stomach because they associate the word cardiac with the heart side rather than with the cardia.
difficulty_basis: One comparison, short interpretation or routine calculation linking up to two prescribed facts

concept_tested: Counting one type of tooth in the complete adult set from the printed dental formula
stem: The adult human dental formula is 2,1,2,3 / 2,1,2,3, the four figures in each half giving the number of incisors, canines, premolars and molars respectively in one half of the upper jaw and one half of the lower jaw. How many premolars are present in the complete adult set?

distractor_rationale.B: 4 is obtained by counting the two premolars of one half of the upper jaw and the two of one half of the lower jaw only, forgetting that each jaw has two halves.
distractor_rationale.C: 12 is the number of molars, obtained by reading the fourth figure of the formula instead of the third.
distractor_rationale.D: 16 is the total number of teeth in one whole jaw, obtained by using the jaw total in place of the premolar count.

solution: The formula gives 2 premolars in one half of the upper jaw and 2 in one half of the lower jaw. Each jaw has two symmetrical halves, so the total is 2 x 2 for the upper jaw plus 2 x 2 for the lower jaw, that is 4 + 4 = 8 premolars.
formula_principle: The dental formula gives the number of each type of tooth in one half of each jaw; the total for a type is the half-jaw figure multiplied by four, since each jaw has two symmetrical halves.
common_misconception: Students read the dental formula as a whole-jaw count rather than a half-jaw count and therefore halve every answer.

concept_tested: Expressing one tooth type as a percentage of the complete adult set using the printed dental formula
stem: The adult human dental formula is 2,1,2,3 / 2,1,2,3, the four figures in each half giving the number of incisors, canines, premolars and molars respectively in one half of the upper jaw and one half of the lower jaw, and the complete set contains 32 teeth. What percentage of the complete set is made up of molars?

distractor_rationale.A: 25 per cent corresponds to 8 teeth out of 32, which is the count of incisors or of premolars, not of molars.
distractor_rationale.C: 12.5 per cent corresponds to 4 teeth out of 32, which is the count of canines.
distractor_rationale.D: 50 per cent corresponds to 16 teeth, which is the number of teeth in one whole jaw rather than the number of molars.

solution: The formula gives 3 molars in one half of the upper jaw and 3 in one half of the lower jaw. Each jaw has two halves, so the total is 3 x 2 + 3 x 2 = 12 molars. As a percentage of the 32 teeth this is (12 / 32) x 100 = 37.5 per cent.
formula_principle: Percentage of a tooth type = (number of that type in the whole set / 32) x 100, where the number of that type is the half-jaw figure multiplied by four.
common_misconception: Students multiply the half-jaw figure by two instead of four, obtaining 6 molars and a percentage of 18.75, or they use the figure for the wrong tooth type.

stem: The duodenum is about 26 cm long, the jejunum about 2.5 metres long and the ileum about 3.5 metres long. Taking 1 metre = 100 cm, what is the sum of these three lengths, expressed in centimetres?

distractor_rationale.A: 600 cm is obtained by adding only the jejunum and the ileum and dropping the duodenum from the sum.
distractor_rationale.B: 656 cm results from converting 2.5 metres to 280 cm by an arithmetic slip while converting the metre values.
distractor_rationale.D: 326 cm results from converting each of 2.5 metres and 3.5 metres to 150 cm and 150 cm, that is from halving the metre figures before conversion.

concept_tested: Distinguishing the cardiac sphincter from the pyloric sphincter by position and by function
stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the cardiac sphincter from the pyloric sphincter?

options.A: The cardiac sphincter regulates passage of material from the stomach to the small intestine, while the pyloric sphincter lies at the junction of the oesophagus and the stomach and prevents regurgitation of food
options.B: The cardiac sphincter is a band of circular muscles at the junction of the oesophagus and the stomach that prevents regurgitation of food, while the pyloric sphincter regulates passage of material from the stomach to the small intestine
options.C: Both sphincters lie at the junction of the oesophagus and the stomach, the cardiac one preventing regurgitation and the pyloric one regulating entry of food
options.D: The cardiac sphincter guards the opening of the hepato-pancreatic duct, while the pyloric sphincter prevents regurgitation of food into the oesophagus

correct_answer_text: The cardiac sphincter is a band of circular muscles at the junction of the oesophagus and the stomach that prevents regurgitation of food, while the pyloric sphincter regulates passage of material from the stomach to the small intestine

distractor_rationale.A: The positions and functions of the two sphincters are interchanged; the cardiac sphincter belongs to the cardia at the oesophageal end.
distractor_rationale.C: The two sphincters guard opposite ends of the stomach; only the cardiac sphincter lies at the oesophageal junction.
distractor_rationale.D: The opening of the hepato-pancreatic duct is guarded by the sphincter of Oddi; neither sphincter of the stomach is concerned with it.

solution: The cardiac sphincter is a band of circular muscles present at the junction of the oesophagus and the stomach and prevents regurgitation of food, whereas the pyloric sphincter is a set of muscles at the pylorus that regulates the passage of material from the stomach into the small intestine.
formula_principle: The stomach is guarded at each end by a sphincter: the cardiac sphincter at the oesophageal junction prevents regurgitation, the pyloric sphincter at the duodenal junction regulates outflow.
common_misconception: Students associate the word cardiac with the far or heart-facing end of the stomach and therefore swap the two sphincters.

stem: Match each term in the first list with the feature it describes in the second list. I. Thecodont II. Diphyodont III. Heterodont IV. Gomphosis P. Presence of four different types of teeth Q. Each tooth fixed in a separate socket present in the jaw bone R. The type of joint by which a tooth is held in its socket S. Only two sets of teeth in a lifetime

distractor_rationale.A: This makes diphyodont mean four types of teeth and heterodont mean two sets of teeth; the two terms are interchanged.
distractor_rationale.C: This makes thecodont mean two sets of teeth and diphyodont mean fixing in separate sockets; the terms for attachment and replacement are interchanged.
distractor_rationale.D: This makes thecodont the name of a joint and gomphosis the fixing in a socket; gomphosis is the joint and thecodont is the condition of being socketed.

solution: Thecodont means each tooth is fixed in a separate socket present in the jaw bones, and the joint by which it is so fixed is called a gomphosis. Diphyodont means only two sets of teeth, milk teeth and permanent teeth, appear in a lifetime. Heterodont means four different types of teeth are present.
formula_principle: Three independent features of human dentition are named separately: thecodont for socketed attachment, diphyodont for two sets in a lifetime, heterodont for four types of teeth; gomphosis names the joint itself.
common_misconception: Students memorise the three terms as a block for human dentition without separating attachment, replacement and variety, and they confuse thecodont with the name of the joint.

concept_tested: Identifying the one named structure of the canal that ends blindly and leads nowhere onward
stem: As a rule, every named region of the alimentary canal opens onward into the next region, so that material entering at the mouth can eventually leave at the anus. One named structure of the canal is an exception, being an outgrowth that does not lead onward into any further region. Which is it?

distractor_rationale.A: The caecum is described as a blind sac, but it lies at the junction of the ileum and colon and material passes on from it into the ascending colon.
distractor_rationale.B: The fundus is a dome shaped region of the stomach continuous with the cardia and the body, so its contents pass on towards the pylorus.
distractor_rationale.C: The rectum temporarily stores undigested waste but opens onward at the anus, the terminal opening of the alimentary canal.

solution: The vermiform appendix is an elongated worm like outgrowth arising from the caecum. It leads on to no further region and is a vestigial organ in human beings, so it is the exception to the through-passage rule.
formula_principle: The alimentary canal is a through tube; the only named structure that arises from it and ends blindly is the vermiform appendix, which is vestigial in human beings.
common_misconception: Students see the word blind in the description of the caecum and choose it, without noticing that the caecum still opens into the colon.
difficulty_basis: Multi-part interpretation, pathway reasoning or calculation linking several facts with plausible traps

stem: The buccal cavity leads into a short pharynx. Which statement about the pharynx is correct?

options.A: It is a passage for food only, air being carried by a separate tube throughout
options.B: It is a common passage for food and air
options.C: It is about 25 cm long and pierces the diaphragm before joining the stomach
options.D: It is lined by a mucosa that is thrown into irregular folds called rugae

stem: A person swallows a morsel of food while lying flat on the back, and the morsel still reaches the stomach. Which property of the oesophagus best explains this?

Within it the oesophagus is about 25 cm, the stomach is taken as 30 cm, the small intestine is about 6 metres and the large intestine is 1.5 metres. stem: In an adult human the dental formula is 2,1,2,3 / 2,1,2,3, the four figures in each half giving the number of incisors, canines, premolars and molars respectively in one half of the upper jaw and one half of the lower jaw, giving 32 teeth in all. If such a person loses all the molars of the lower jaw only, how many teeth and how many tooth-to-socket gomphosis joints remain?

distractor_rationale.A: The tooth count is right but the joint count is not reduced; each lost tooth also removes its own socket joint, since there is one gomphosis joint per tooth.

stem: Pancreatic juice reaches the duodenum carrying the inactive enzyme trypsinogen, while enterokinase is present in the intestinal juice. Suppose the intestinal glands fail to supply enterokinase while the pancreas goes on secreting normally. What would happen in the small intestine?

options.B: Trypsinogen would no longer be secreted by the pancreas
options.C: Trypsinogen would be converted into trypsin by the bile salts instead
options.D: Trypsin would still be formed, since the pancreas secretes it in the active form

options.C: Cholecystokinin stimulates the secretion of gastric juice and suppresses the feeling of fullness

concept_tested: Matching each named mechanism of absorption with the substance it moves and its stated requirement
stem: Match the mechanism of absorption in column I with its description in column II. I. Simple diffusion, II. Facilitated transport, III. Active transport, IV. Osmosis. P. Absorption of sodium against the concentration gradient, requiring energy. Q. Absorption of water along the concentration gradient. R. Absorption of part of the glucose and of chloride ions, depending on the concentration gradient. S. Absorption of fructose with the help of carrier ions like Na+.

distractor_rationale.A: The carrier-assisted uptake of fructose is placed under simple diffusion, although simple diffusion needs no carrier.
distractor_rationale.C: Water movement along the gradient is labelled active transport, although active transport is defined by movement against the gradient with expenditure of energy.

common_misconception: Students confuse facilitated transport with active transport because both involve a carrier, and overlook that only active transport works against the gradient and needs energy.

concept_tested: Computing the energy actually produced by a meal from the physiological values per gram
stem: The physiological value of food is the actual energy produced by 1 g of it. These values are 4.0 Kcal/g for carbohydrate, 4.0 Kcal/g for protein and 9.0 Kcal/g for fat. A meal supplies 20 g of carbohydrate, 10 g of protein and 5 g of fat. What is the total energy actually produced by this meal?

distractor_rationale.A: The gross calorific value 4.1 Kcal/g has been used for the carbohydrate instead of its physiological value 4.0 Kcal/g.
distractor_rationale.B: The gross calorific value 5.65 Kcal/g has been used for the protein although the question asks for the energy actually produced.
distractor_rationale.D: The gross calorific values 4.1, 5.65 and 9.45 Kcal/g have been used throughout, which gives the heat of combustion and not the energy actually produced.

solution: Using the physiological values, the carbohydrate gives 20 x 4.0 = 80 Kcal, the protein gives 10 x 4.0 = 40 Kcal and the fat gives 5 x 9.0 = 45 Kcal, so the meal produces 80 + 40 + 45 = 165 Kcal.
formula_principle: Energy produced equals the sum over each food type of mass in grams multiplied by the physiological value in Kcal per gram.
common_misconception: Students use the gross calorific value, which is the heat liberated on complete combustion of 1 g of food in a bomb calorimeter, when the energy actually produced by the body is asked for.

concept_tested: Computing by how much the gross calorific value of a portion exceeds its physiological value
stem: For 1 g of food the gross calorific values are 4.1 Kcal/g for carbohydrate, 5.65 Kcal/g for protein and 9.45 Kcal/g for fat, while the physiological values are 4.0 Kcal/g for carbohydrate, 4.0 Kcal/g for protein and 9.0 Kcal/g for fat. A portion of food contains 50 g of carbohydrate, 20 g of protein and 10 g of fat. By how much does the gross calorific value of this portion exceed its physiological value?

distractor_rationale.B: The difference of 0.45 Kcal/g for the 10 g of fat has been left out of the total.
distractor_rationale.C: The difference of 0.1 Kcal/g for the 50 g of carbohydrate has been dismissed as negligible and omitted.
distractor_rationale.D: Only the protein difference has been counted, on the assumption that carbohydrate and fat show no gap between the two values.

solution: The per gram differences are 4.1 - 4.0 = 0.1 Kcal/g for carbohydrate, 5.65 - 4.0 = 1.65 Kcal/g for protein and 9.45 - 9.0 = 0.45 Kcal/g for fat. The excess is therefore 50 x 0.1 = 5 Kcal plus 20 x 1.65 = 33 Kcal plus 10 x 0.45 = 4.5 Kcal, giving 42.5 Kcal.
formula_principle: The excess equals the sum over each food type of mass in grams multiplied by the difference between its gross calorific value and its physiological value per gram.
common_misconception: Students treat gross calorific value and physiological value as the same quantity for carbohydrate and fat because the two figures are close, and count only the protein gap.

concept_tested: Deducing the consequence of the body being unable to store excess amino acids
stem: The body can store excess carbohydrates and fats but cannot store excess amino acids. What follows from this for the handling of a protein rich meal?

options.A: The surplus amino acids are stored in the liver and released again only when the diet is short of protein
options.B: The surplus amino acids are excreted unchanged, so that no nitrogenous waste has to be formed at all
options.C: The surplus amino acids are deaminated, and the ammonia formed is either excreted as such or converted into urea or uric acid
options.D: The surplus amino acids are converted into fat, so that no nitrogenous waste is produced from them

correct_answer_text: The surplus amino acids are deaminated, and the ammonia formed is either excreted as such or converted into urea or uric acid

distractor_rationale.A: This is the very storage that the body cannot perform for amino acids, although it can store surplus carbohydrate and fat.
distractor_rationale.B: Excretion of the intact amino acid is not the route described; the amino group is first separated by deamination and appears as ammonia.
distractor_rationale.D: The nitrogen of the amino group cannot be absorbed into a fat store; it must leave the body as ammonia, urea or uric acid.

solution: Carbohydrate and fat can be stored, but surplus amino acids cannot. They are therefore deaminated, the amino group being separated to yield ammonia, and that ammonia is either excreted directly or converted into urea or uric acid.
formula_principle: Since excess amino acids cannot be stored, they are deaminated, and the ammonia so formed is excreted as such or converted into urea or uric acid.
common_misconception: Students assume that an amino acid surplus is simply stored, or converted wholly into fat, and forget that the nitrogen must be excreted.

concept_tested: Classifying two substances that leave by the same route but have different origins
stem: Excretion is the elimination of metabolic waste products formed inside the body cells; egestion is the removal of substances that have never entered the cells; secretion is the release of a product that the body puts to use. Bilirubin and undigested residue both leave the body in the faeces. Using these definitions, which classification is correct?

options.A: Bilirubin leaving in the faeces is excretion, while undigested residue leaving in the faeces is egestion
options.B: Bilirubin leaving in the faeces is secretion, while undigested residue leaving in the faeces is excretion
options.C: Bilirubin leaving in the faeces is egestion, while undigested residue leaving in the faeces is excretion
options.D: Bilirubin and undigested residue leaving in the faeces are both egestion, because they share the same route

correct_answer_text: Bilirubin leaving in the faeces is excretion, while undigested residue leaving in the faeces is egestion

distractor_rationale.B: Bilirubin is a waste of haemoglobin breakdown and is not put to use by the body, and undigested residue never entered the cells at all.
distractor_rationale.C: The two are exactly interchanged; bilirubin is formed inside the body while the residue has never entered any cell.
distractor_rationale.D: This classifies by route rather than by origin, which is the distinction the definitions actually rest on.

solution: Bilirubin is formed within the body from the breakdown of haemoglobin, so its removal is excretion even though it leaves in the faeces. Undigested residue has never entered the body cells, so its removal is egestion.
formula_principle: Excretion, secretion and egestion are distinguished by the origin and fate of the substance, not by the route of exit: a metabolic waste formed in cells is excreted whatever route it takes.
common_misconception: Students classify by the route of exit and therefore call everything leaving in the faeces the same kind of process.

concept_tested: Reasoning from urea retention in sharks to its osmotic consequence
stem: Sharks retain a large quantity of urea in their body fluid instead of eliminating all of it. What does this retention achieve?

options.A: It makes their blood hypotonic to the surrounding sea water and so speeds up the entry of water into the body
options.B: It makes their blood hypertonic to the surrounding sea water and so drives excess salts out through the gills
options.C: It makes their blood isotonic to fresh water and so prevents the entry of salts from the sea
options.D: It makes their blood isotonic to the surrounding sea water and so prevents the loss of water by exosmosis

correct_answer_text: It makes their blood isotonic to the surrounding sea water and so prevents the loss of water by exosmosis

distractor_rationale.C: Sharks are marine, so the reference fluid is sea water; matching the blood to fresh water would not solve their osmotic problem.
